The lean adds weight to the steering axle and always improves control
questions.explanation: Keep the load centered, not piled on one wall. Off-center freight overloads one side and raises rollover risk. Block it so it cannot slide farther sideways. The trailer leans, one side's tires and axles carry too much, and a curve can roll the rig more easily.
questions.why: An off-center load that makes the trailer lean makes a rollover more likely.

provenance.manual: AAMVA Commercial Driver's License Manual (2025 CDL Testing System)

questions.q: You tightened the chains, but the winch or binder can still be moved by hand and the chain is slack. May you count that tiedown?
options: Yes, if the hook is on the door latch
No. A loose binder is not secure
Yes. Any chain on the deck counts, slack or not
Yes, if you will bounce it tight within 100 miles
questions.explanation: Securement devices have to be tight before you move. Slack means the device is not restraining the cargo. Fix it at the pre-trip, not at some later made-up mileage. No. A loose winch or an open, untensioned binder is not a secure tiedown.

questions.q: During the inspection inside the first 50 miles you find a binder that vibrated open. What is the rule you are applying?
options: Leave it, because the before-driving inspection was the last required look
Replace the binder with the door latch
Stop and secure it now
Close it only if you have already passed 150 miles
questions.explanation: Inspect before you drive, then again within 50 miles, specifically so devices that loosen on the road get caught. After that, keep the 3-hour or 150-mile schedule and the duty-status checks. That early recheck is required, and it does not replace the later 3-hour or 150-mile checks.
questions.remember: Loose strap? Fix it right away.

questions.q: A group of cartons weighs 8,000 pounds. What aggregate working load limit must the tiedown system reach?
options: At least 8,000 pounds plus another 8,000 for safety
At least 800 pounds, one tenth of the weight
No minimum, if you used the right number of straps
At least 4,000 pounds, half the weight of that cargo
questions.explanation: The aggregate working load limit must be at least half the weight of the article or group. Half of 8,000 is 4,000. Count and strength are separate requirements.
questions.remember: Tiedowns hold at least half the weight.

questions.q: Two straps each have a 2,000-pound working load limit, but one strap's hook is stamped far lower, at 500 pounds. How do you treat that strap?
options: Rate it at 500 pounds, its weakest part
Rate it at 2,000
Rate it at 2,500 by adding the hook to the webbing
Drop it from the count and hook the cargo to the door latch instead
questions.explanation: The weakest part sets the tiedown's limit. A 500-pound hook makes the assembly a 500-pound tiedown no matter what the webbing says. Rate that strap at 500 pounds, the weakest component, and do not pretend it still offers 2,000.
questions.remember: A tiedown is as strong as its weakest part.

questions.q: Can a headerboard by itself satisfy the rule for a tall load that can still tip sideways?
options: Yes, whenever the load is unblocked and longer than 10 feet
No. It must not slide sideways or back either
Yes. Headerboards are rated to stop motion in every direction
Yes, if the headerboard is taller than the load even when the load does not touch it
questions.explanation: A headerboard addresses forward movement, and only if the cargo is against it. You still need blocking, bracing, or tiedowns for rearward and sideways movement. No. Forward blocking is only one direction. Brace and tie the load so it cannot slide sideways or rearward either.

questions.q: Putting too much of the load over the drives and the trailer, and almost nothing on the steer axle, produces what?
options: Sharper, heavier steering feel from extra front grip
Immunity from overweight citations on the rear axles
A shorter stopping distance than a balanced load
A wandering, hard-to-steer truck
questions.explanation: Too little weight on the steering axle makes the truck wander and hard to steer. Move weight forward or adjust the tandems, then reweigh. Do not overload the steer axle in the process.
questions.why: Too little weight on the front axle makes steering unsafe.
questions.remember: Too light up front: hard to steer.

provenance.manual: AAMVA Commercial Driver's License Manual (2025 CDL Testing System)

questions.q: A partial liquid load starts to shove the tractor after you have already released the brake. What are you feeling?
options: A normal feeling that means you should brake harder next time
Surge from the liquid still moving
A baffle that has removed all liquid movement
Proof that a half-full tank is more stable than a full one
questions.explanation: Surge continues after the vehicle changes speed. Partial loads do this more than full tanks. Smooth, early brake applications reduce the size of the wave you have to manage. Surge. The liquid is still moving even though your brake application has changed.
questions.why: Liquid moving in a part-full tank pushes the truck.

provenance.manual: AAMVA Commercial Driver's License Manual (2025 CDL Testing System)

questions.q: Which comparison of tank loads is correct?
options: Baffles make a half-full tank surge-free
Surge is only a problem when the tank is empty
A half-full tank surges more than a full one
A full tank surges more
questions.explanation: Empty space is what lets liquid travel. A full tank has little room to surge. Baffles cut forward and backward movement but do not erase surge, and a half-full smooth bore is worse.
questions.why: Liquid moving in a part-full tank pushes the truck.

provenance.manual: AAMVA Commercial Driver's License Manual (2025 CDL Testing System)

questions.q: Baffles are installed crosswise in the tank. Which claim is too strong?
options: The claim that baffles reduce front-to-back surge
The claim that a partial load can still move and shift the weight of the vehicle
The claim that smooth braking still matters
The claim that baffles remove surge completely and let you steer or brake like a dry van
questions.explanation: Say what baffles do, not more. They reduce forward and backward surge. They do not remove it, side-to-side surge still occurs, and they do not cancel the need for smooth braking and steering.
questions.why: Baffles slow front-to-back surge; side-to-side surge can still happen.

provenance.manual: AAMVA Commercial Driver's License Manual (2025 CDL Testing System)

questions.q: An article 5 feet long is blocked tight against the bulkhead. Which count is allowed by the working rule?
options: One, if it is strong enough
At least five tiedowns, one per foot
At least two
None, if the bulkhead is taller than the article
questions.explanation: Blocked against forward movement, an article needs one tiedown for every 10 feet of length or fraction, so one satisfies the count here. A 10-foot piece that is not blocked still needs at least two. Strength must still be at least half the cargo weight.
questions.remember: Blocked in front? Fewer tiedowns needed.

questions.q: The same 5-foot article weighs 1,500 pounds, and nothing blocks it forward. What count now?
options: One tiedown on the door latch
At least two tiedowns
One tiedown, because it is short, whether or not it is blocked
Zero tiedowns, because short freight cannot shift
questions.explanation: Without forward blocking, a piece 5 feet or shorter can use one tiedown only if it weighs 1,100 pounds or less. At 1,500 pounds it needs at least two.

questions.q: A 30-foot unblocked timber needs how many tiedowns at minimum?
options: At least one, placed in the center
At least six, and two of them must use the door latch
At least four
At least three
questions.explanation: Two tiedowns cover the first 10 feet, and each additional 10 feet or fraction adds one. The extra 20 feet adds two, so the minimum is four. Strength is a separate requirement.

questions.q: A 16-foot article is blocked against the headerboard. Using the blocked-length rule, how many tiedowns are required?
options: One for the whole 16 feet
Sixteen tiny straps in place of rated tiedowns
Three, two for the first 10 feet plus one more
Two, one for each 10 feet or fraction
questions.explanation: Blocked cargo needs one tiedown for every 10 feet of length or fraction. Sixteen feet is one unit plus a fraction, so the minimum is two.
questions.remember: Blocked in front? Fewer tiedowns needed.

questions.q: Which mistake treats a headerboard as magic?
options: Counting it as forward blocking even though the cargo does not touch it
Refusing to count it when the crates are tight against it
Still using tiedowns after the cargo is blocked forward
Checking that its welds and uprights are sound
questions.explanation: Contact is the test. If the freight is not against the headerboard, bulkhead, or other cargo, it is not blocked forward, and the unblocked tiedown count applies.
questions.remember: Blocked in front? Fewer tiedowns needed.

questions.q: You have a sharp corner, a loose winch, and an open binder on the same load. What do those three defects share?
options: All three can be ignored on a sealed trailer
None of them is secure tiedown equipment in that condition
All three are acceptable during the first 50 miles
All three are fixed by moving the hook to the door latch
questions.explanation: Tiedowns must be tight, binders closed and tensioned, and straps protected from sharp edges. Any one of those failures means the cargo is not secured for the trip. The truck should not move until they are fixed.

questions.q: A leaking drum is inside a van and fluid is running out the door sill. What is required?
options: Contain the leak before you go back on the road
Leave the doors cracked so the fluid air-dries on the highway
Call it a seal issue only, and ignore the fluid
Pour absorbent on the road and keep driving
questions.explanation: Leaking cargo has to be contained. A visible leak is not something a seal rule lets you ignore, and it is not something you drip down the highway.
questions.remember: Nothing leaks, spills, blows or falls.

questions.q: How should heavy machinery sit relative to the trailer's centerline and floor?
options: Ahead of the tractor's bumper so the steer axle is obviously overloaded
Low, centered, and near the middle lengthwise
High on cribbing at the extreme rear, biased to one side
Against the doors, unblocked, with one loose strap
questions.explanation: Low and centered keeps the center of gravity down and the axle weights usable. Slightly forward of the trailer center lets forward blocking work, as long as you do not overload the steering axle.
questions.why: Cargo piled high makes you more likely to tip over.

provenance.manual: AAMVA Commercial Driver's License Manual (2025 CDL Testing System)

questions.q: Overloading and poor placement can lengthen stopping distance and also do what to the steering axle?
options: Both errors always take it off the bridge formula
Placement cannot change steering-axle weight
Too far back can lighten it
Both errors always lighten it
questions.explanation: Where the weight sits changes steer-axle load. Too little makes the truck wander and hard to steer. Too much is an overweight axle. The whole combination also takes longer to stop if it is overloaded.
questions.why: Too little weight on the front axle makes steering unsafe.
questions.remember: Too light up front: hard to steer.

provenance.manual: AAMVA Commercial Driver's License Manual (2025 CDL Testing System)

questions.q: You changed from sleeper berth to on-duty not driving to adjust chains. Which cargo inspection duty applies?
options: Duty-status changes cancel cargo checks for the rest of the day
Inspect only if the change happens after 100 miles
Skip it, because sleeper berth time secures the freight by itself
Inspect at that change of duty status, and fix any loose tiedown before you drive
questions.explanation: Every change of duty status is an inspection point for cargo securement. Adjusting chains is useless if you do not actually confirm they are tight and the load has not shifted.
questions.remember: Recheck the load as you go.

questions.q: Which statement correctly combines the 50-mile check with the later schedule?
options: It is extra and does not replace later checks
Once you complete the 50-mile check you may skip the 3-hour and 150-mile checks
The 50-mile check is optional if you plan to stop every 100 miles
The first time you must look at the cargo is at mile 50
questions.explanation: Order matters. Inspect before you drive. Inspect again within the first 50 miles. Then continue every 3 hours or 150 miles, whichever comes first, and at every change of duty status. The 50-mile check is an extra early reinspection, and it does not replace the later checks every 3 hours or 150 miles, whichever comes first.
questions.remember: Recheck the load as you go.

questions.q: A driver plans the first cargo look for mile 49 and does not look in the yard. What did the driver skip?
options: The 100-mile recheck
The required inspection before the vehicle is driven
Nothing, because any look before mile 50 satisfies the whole rule
Only the weekly bridge inspection
questions.explanation: The first inspection is before you drive. The inspection within the first 50 miles is the second one. Starting the trip and waiting until you are already on the road does not satisfy the before-driving duty.
questions.remember: Check the load before you drive.

questions.q: Tiedown hardware is rated, but the trailer's anchor point is cracked and obviously weaker than the strap. What limits that tiedown?
options: The door latch you could use instead of the cracked anchor
Nothing, if the count of straps is correct
The damaged anchor
The strap tag alone
questions.explanation: The assembly includes the anchor. If the anchor is the weak point, the tiedown's limit drops to what that anchor can hold. A cracked point is not a secure attachment. The weakest part sets the working load limit.
questions.remember: A tiedown is as strong as its weakest part.

questions.q: You added edge protection, but you are still one tiedown short of the count and under half the cargo weight in total strength. What did the edge protection change?
options: It doubles the count of every strap it touches
It removes the need for blocking in every direction
It lets you hook the shortfall to the door latch
It only protects the straps you have
questions.explanation: Edge protection keeps a strap from being cut. You still need the right number of tiedowns and an aggregate working load limit of at least half the cargo weight.
questions.remember: Tiedowns hold at least half the weight.

questions.q: Which load of liquid needs the most cautious braking and steering?
options: A half-full smooth-bore tank with no baffles
A completely full tank with almost no free space
An empty tank that has been drained and dried
A half-full tank whose baffles you treat as having removed all surge
questions.explanation: Partial loads surge more than full loads, and a smooth bore without baffles lets the liquid travel farther. Baffles would only reduce forward and backward surge, not delete it.

provenance.manual: AAMVA Commercial Driver's License Manual (2025 CDL Testing System)

questions.q: While climbing a ramp you feel the rig start to feel light in the steering after a hard brake. The freight is stacked at the rear. What is the likely cargo cause?
options: Baffles in a dry van removing traction
Too little weight on the steering axle
Too much weight on the steering axle from rear freight
A posted bridge limit changing the steering feel
questions.explanation: Rear-heavy freight unloads the front axle. The truck then wanders and is hard to steer. Move the heavy cargo forward, low, and near the center, and block it. The load sits too far back.
questions.why: Too little weight on the front axle makes steering unsafe.
questions.remember: Too light up front: hard to steer.

provenance.manual: AAMVA Commercial Driver's License Manual (2025 CDL Testing System)

questions.q: A shipper loaded heavy coils high, against the left wall, and ahead of the kingpin area so the steer axle is over its limit. Name the problems.
options: Only the left-wall placement matters, and height and steer weight are fine
The steer axle cannot be overloaded if the coils are in the tractor's shadow
High and off-center freight raises rollover risk, and the steering axle is overweight
That placement is ideal
questions.explanation: Heavy freight belongs low and centered, only slightly forward of the trailer center when that helps blocking. Too far forward overloads the steering axle. High, one-sided freight rolls more easily.
questions.remember: Too heavy up front: hard steering.

provenance.manual: AAMVA Commercial Driver's License Manual (2025 CDL Testing System)

questions.q: Must tiedowns be rechecked only when they look damaged, or on a schedule even if they looked fine earlier?
options: Only when a strap is already broken in two
Only every 100 miles, and only on flatbeds
Only at the annual inspection
On the federal schedule, even if fine
questions.explanation: Waiting for an obvious failure is not the rule. The inspections are timed so you find a shift or a loosening device before it becomes a road hazard. On the schedule: before driving, within 50 miles, then every 3 hours or 150 miles, whichever comes first, and at every duty-status change.
questions.remember: Recheck the load as you go.

questions.q: A 10-foot unblocked skid is held by one new strap with a huge working load limit. Why is that still not enough?
options: Unblocked pieces need at least two tiedowns
Strength replaces count, so one very strong strap is always legal
Ten-foot pieces are limited to one tiedown by the blocked-cargo rule
A high rating lets you attach that one strap to the door latch
questions.explanation: Count and strength are both minimums. One strap fails the unblocked count for a 10-foot piece even if its working load limit is enormous. Use at least two, and still reach half the cargo weight in aggregate. The count requires at least two tiedowns when the piece is not blocked, no matter how strong the single strap is.

questions.q: A 4-foot blocked crate has one tiedown whose working load limit is well above half the crate's weight. What else must still be true?
options: The door latch should be the anchor for that one tiedown
It must truly be blocked against forward movement
The single tiedown is enough even if the crate sits two feet off the headerboard
Sideways movement can be ignored
questions.explanation: The one-tiedown option is only for a short piece that is really blocked forward. You still have to stop rearward and sideways sliding, and the tiedown has to be tight and strong enough. The crate must actually be against the headerboard, bulkhead, or other cargo that stops forward movement, and it must not be free to slide back or sideways.
questions.remember: Blocked in front? Fewer tiedowns needed.

questions.q: Which placement best matches a heavy pallet that must be blocked from sliding forward?
options: On one side, unsecured
In the cab, unsecured
Low, centered, and touching the headerboard
High, at the rear doors, with daylight between it and the headerboard
questions.explanation: Slightly forward of center lets the forward block work and keeps the weight low. The pallet has to touch that block. Leaving a gap means the headerboard is not blocking it.
questions.why: Cargo piled high makes you more likely to tip over.

provenance.manual: AAMVA Commercial Driver's License Manual (2025 CDL Testing System)

questions.q: Cargo securement fails if the freight can move, even when you used expensive hardware. Which result is the actual goal?
options: The hardware was purchased new this year
The doors are latched
The gross weight is written on the bill of lading
The freight cannot shift, blow, or fall off
questions.explanation: Devices are a means. The result required is cargo that stays on the vehicle and does not shift. Cover or contain what can blow or leak, and block what can slide. The freight cannot slide forward, back, or sideways, and it cannot blow, leak, or fall off.
questions.remember: Nothing leaks, spills, blows or falls.

questions.q: You will enter a state scale in 10 miles, and you have not weighed the axles. What is the professional move?
options: Weigh now and fix any axle before the scale
Assume the shipper's guess is exact and keep going
Slide the tandems forward or back at random without reweighing
Ignore a posted bridge on the way
questions.explanation: Know your weights before enforcement or a bridge does it for you. A posted bridge limit still controls that bridge even if you are under your registered gross. Weigh the axles and the gross now, and fix a too-light steer axle or an overweight axle before the scale.
questions.remember: Know the weight before you take it.

provenance.manual: AAMVA Commercial Driver's License Manual (2025 CDL Testing System)

questions.q: A half-full tank and a full tank of the same product are both legal weight. Which one demands more space in front of you?
options: The half-full tank only if it has no liquid in it
The half-full tank
The full tank
Neither, because baffles always remove surge in both tanks
questions.explanation: More free surface means more surge. Give the partial load earlier, smoother braking and more following distance than you would need for a full, settled tank.
questions.why: Liquid moving in a part-full tank pushes the truck.

provenance.manual: AAMVA Commercial Driver's License Manual (2025 CDL Testing System)

questions.q: After a panic stop you see the load has walked forward into a gap you left in front of the headerboard. What should you change before driving again?
options: Leave the new position
Add only a door-latch hook and depart
Wait until 100 miles later to see if it walks back
Move it back to the brace and retighten
questions.explanation: The gap meant the headerboard was not blocking anything. Put the cargo against the block, tie it tight, and brace it so it cannot come back or slide sideways. Reposition the freight against the headerboard or another forward brace, retighten the tiedowns, and block the other directions.
questions.remember: Blocked in front? Fewer tiedowns needed.

questions.q: Federal cargo checks include a look at securement devices you can see on a sealed van. Which device problem must stop the trip?
options: A loose, cut, or dragging tiedown
A scuff in the paint on the landing gear
A seal number you have already written on the bill
Mud on the tandem mudflaps
questions.explanation: You do not break the seal to rummage, but you do not haul a dragging strap, a cut tiedown you can see, a leak, or a leaning trailer. Fix visible securement failures before you move.
questions.remember: Everything that holds the load secured.

questions.q: Which sentence states the steer-axle lesson without mixing it up with bridge law?
options: Bridge limits apply only when the steer axle is light
Too little steer-axle weight makes the truck wander and hard to steer
Too little steer-axle weight is legal as long as the bridge is posted
Too much steer-axle weight improves steering and cancels bridge postings
questions.explanation: Three separate rules: enough weight to steer, no axle over its limit, and obedience to a posted bridge even when the truck is otherwise legal. Too much weight on any axle, including the steer axle, is an overweight violation; a posted bridge limit still controls that bridge.
questions.why: Too little weight on the front axle makes steering unsafe.
questions.remember: Too light up front: hard to steer.

provenance.manual: AAMVA Commercial Driver's License Manual (2025 CDL Testing System)

questions.q: A 6-foot article blocked by other secured cargo needs how many tiedowns under the working rule?
options: Six, one per foot
Zero, because blocked cargo can ride with no tiedowns
One, since blocked cargo needs one per 10 feet
Two, because it is longer than 5 feet
questions.explanation: Blocked cargo needs one tiedown for every 10 feet of length or fraction, so a 6-foot blocked article needs one, plus enough working load limit and restraint in every direction. Blocking never means zero tiedowns.
questions.remember: Blocked in front? Fewer tiedowns needed.

questions.q: An unblocked 40-foot beam is on the deck. What is the minimum tiedown count?
options: At least two tiedowns
At least four tiedowns
At least eight tiedowns, two of them on the door latch
At least five tiedowns
questions.explanation: Two tiedowns cover the first 10 feet, plus one for each additional 10 feet or fraction. The extra 30 feet adds three, for five in all. Do not stop at a one-per-ten count.

questions.q: What should you do with a tiedown that meets the count on paper but is twisted, slack, and running over an unprotected sharp edge?
options: Do not count it as secure
Count it, because the pre-trip only checks that a strap exists
Wait until mile 100 and then decide
Move the hook to the door latch so the edge no longer matters
questions.explanation: A loose winch, an open binder, or a strap over a sharp edge with no protection is not secure. Existence is not tension, and tension without protection can fail as soon as the load shifts. Protect, untwist, and tension it, or replace it, before you move.

questions.q: You finished loading, closed the doors, and have not looked at the freight securement. The shipper is waving you out. What is your duty?
options: Skip inspections because the shipper watched you load
Inspect before driving and again within 50 miles
Leave now and make the first inspection at mile 50
Leave now and make the first inspection at mile 100
questions.explanation: Nobody else's hurry cancels the before-driving inspection. The within-50-miles look is additional. Do not make the 50-mile point your first look.
questions.remember: Check the load early in the trip.

questions.q: Liquid cargo without a tank endorsement question attached: what is the practical driving point about a half-full tank?
options: Baffles remove side-to-side and longitudinal surge completely
Surge only matters on hazmat loads
It surges more, so brake and steer smoothly
It surges less than a full tank
questions.explanation: You do not need a tank-endorsement trick to remember this. Partial loads surge more. Baffles reduce forward and backward surge and do not remove it, and side-to-side surge still occurs. Smooth inputs and extra space are the control.
questions.why: Liquid moving in a part-full tank pushes the truck.

provenance.manual: AAMVA Commercial Driver's License Manual (2025 CDL Testing System)

questions.q: A loaded truck takes longer to stop than it did when you scaled a lighter legal load the day before. What cargo fact explains that?
options: Overloading, or simply more weight, lengthens braking distance
Heavier loads always stop shorter
Stopping distance changes only with baffle settings
Weight has no relationship to braking once the tiedown count is met
questions.explanation: More weight takes more distance to stop. An overload makes that worse and can also upset axle loads and steering. Secure the freight and weigh it.

provenance.manual: AAMVA Commercial Driver's License Manual (2025 CDL Testing System)

questions.q: A property-carrying driver who just finished 10 consecutive hours off duty may drive for how long?
options: Up to 10 hours
As long as the weekly clock has time, with no daily driving cap
Up to 11 hours, and only inside the 14-hour window that follows that break
Up to 14 hours of driving
questions.explanation: Property-carrying drivers may drive a maximum of 11 hours after 10 consecutive hours off duty. Those 11 hours must also fit inside the 14-hour window. The passenger 10-hour driving limit is a different rule.

questions.q: Came on duty at 6 a.m. after 10 hours off and has driven 11 hours by late afternoon. May this property-carrying driver keep rolling until the 14th hour?
options: Yes. The 14-hour window allows 14 hours of driving
Yes, if a 20-minute break is logged before the next mile
Yes. Midnight will reset the 11-hour clock automatically
No. The 11-hour driving limit is used up
questions.explanation: Hitting 11 hours of driving stops driving even if the 14-hour window still has time. A short break does not restore those 11 hours, and a new calendar day does not reset them. No. The 11-hour driving limit is already used, so more driving has to wait for a new qualifying break.

questions.q: It is the 14th hour after this property-carrying driver came on duty, and 3 driving hours remain on the 11-hour clock. What is allowed?
options: No more driving
Three more hours of driving
Three more hours if the driver takes a 20-minute off-duty break first
Driving until the weekly 70-hour total is reached, ignoring the 14
questions.explanation: You may not drive after the 14th hour from the end of the last qualifying 10-hour break. Leftover driving time cannot be used. A 20-minute break does not extend the 14-hour clock. The 14-hour window has run out even though driving time is left.

questions.q: This property-carrying driver took a 20-minute off-duty break at midday. Does that break push the end of the 14-hour window back by 20 minutes?
options: Yes. Any break of at least 15 minutes restarts the 14
No. Ordinary off-duty breaks inside the day do not extend the 14-hour clock
Yes. Every off-duty minute pauses the 14-hour window
Yes, but only if the 20 minutes are logged as sleeper berth
questions.explanation: The 14-hour window runs straight through ordinary breaks. A 20-minute stop does not add time to it. Only a qualifying 10-hour break, or a valid split-sleeper pair, changes that daily calculation.

questions.q: Four hours were spent on duty, not driving, while the trailer was loaded. How do those hours treat a property-carrying driver's clocks?
options: They pause the 14-hour window until the driver starts moving
They reset both the 11-hour and 14-hour clocks
They count toward the 14 and 60/70, not the 11
They reduce the 11-hour driving limit by four hours and do not touch the 14
questions.explanation: On-duty not driving is still on duty. It uses the 14-hour window and the weekly on-duty limit. It is not driving, so it does not count against the 11-hour driving limit.

questions.q: Because loading used 4 on-duty hours, how many driving hours can still fit before the 14-hour window ends?
options: Still 11 driving hours
Fourteen more driving hours, measured from the end of loading
Only 4 driving hours
At most 10 hours of driving
questions.explanation: The 14-hour window does not pause for on-duty loading. Four hours of it are already gone, so no more than 10 hours of driving can fit before the window ends, whichever of the 11 or the 14 you hit first. At most 10 hours of driving, even though the 11-hour driving limit would otherwise allow 11.

questions.q: After 8 cumulative hours of driving, a property-carrying driver stopped for 20 minutes. Is that the required break?
options: No. The break must be 30 consecutive minutes
Yes. Any stop after the 8th driving hour, even 10 minutes, is enough
Yes. Twenty minutes off duty resets the 11-hour and 14-hour clocks
No. The only legal break is 10 consecutive hours off duty right then
questions.explanation: The break after 8 cumulative hours of driving is at least 30 consecutive minutes. A 20-minute stop does not satisfy it and does not reset the 11-hour or 14-hour clocks. No. Before driving again the driver needs at least 30 consecutive minutes off duty, in the sleeper, or on duty not driving.

questions.q: A property-carrying driver fuels and does paperwork on duty, not driving, for 35 consecutive minutes after 8 hours of driving. Does that count as the required break?
options: No. Only sleeper-berth time can ever count as the break
Yes, but it does not reset the 11 or the 14
No. The 30 minutes must be spent off duty and cannot be on duty at all
Yes. Those 35 minutes also restart the 14-hour window
questions.explanation: The 30-minute interruption of driving may be off duty, sleeper berth, or on-duty not driving. It allows more driving only if the 11-hour and 14-hour limits still have time. It does not reset either clock.

questions.q: Eight hours of driving were followed by a 15-minute break, more driving, and another 15-minute break. Is the 30-minute rule met?
options: Yes. Fifteen minutes is the property-carrying standard once you pass 8 driving hours
No break is required if the two stops are both logged off duty
No. The 30 minutes must be consecutive, not two shorter breaks with driving between them
Yes. Any minutes that add to 30 across the day satisfy the rule
questions.explanation: The interruption has to be at least 30 consecutive minutes. Split pieces with driving in between do not add up. Take the full 30 before you drive again.

questions.q: What does the 30-minute break do to the 11-hour driving limit and the 14-hour window for a property-carrying driver?
options: It resets the 11-hour clock and leaves the 14 unchanged
It resets the 14-hour window and leaves the 11 unchanged
It restarts the 60-hour or 70-hour weekly clock
It does not reset either one
questions.explanation: A 30-minute break is not a 10-hour break and it is not a 34-hour restart. Driving time already used stays used, and the 14-hour window keeps the time it has already consumed. It only interrupts driving so you may drive again if both limits still allow it.

questions.q: The carrier does not operate commercial vehicles every day of the week. Which weekly on-duty limit applies to this property-carrying driver?
options: 60 hours in 7 consecutive days
70 hours in 8 consecutive days
60 hours of driving only, with on-duty not driving excluded
No weekly limit if each day stays inside 11 driving hours
questions.explanation: When the carrier does not run every day, the property-carrying limit is 60 on-duty hours in any 7 consecutive days. The 70-hour, 8-day rule is for carriers that operate every day of the week.
questions.remember: Not every day: 60 hours in 7 days.

questions.q: This carrier operates commercial vehicles every day of the week. Which weekly limit applies to its property-carrying drivers?
options: 70 hours of driving, with loading time excluded
70 hours on duty in 8 consecutive days
60 hours on duty in 7 consecutive days, even though the carrier runs daily
80 hours on duty in 8 consecutive days
questions.explanation: If the carrier operates every day of the week, the property-carrying limit is 70 on-duty hours in 8 consecutive days. That total includes on-duty not driving, not driving alone.

questions.q: Ten consecutive hours off duty have just ended for a property-carrying driver. Which clocks restart, and which do not?
options: The 60/70-hour clock restarts, but the 11 and 14 do not
Nothing restarts unless the 10 hours included a 34-hour restart
The 11-hour and 14-hour clocks restart
Only the 30-minute break restarts, and the 11 and 14 keep running
questions.explanation: Ten consecutive hours off duty is the daily reset for the 11-hour driving limit and the 14-hour window. Weekly on-duty hours remain until they age out or a 34-hour restart is taken.

questions.q: How must the 10 hours off duty be arranged before a property-carrying driver may start a new 11-hour and 14-hour period?
options: Any 10 hours off duty in the calendar day, even with driving in between
Eight consecutive hours are enough if the driver feels rested
A 4-hour nap plus a later 6-hour nap, with driving between them, is the standard reset
They must be 10 consecutive hours off duty
questions.explanation: The daily break is consecutive. Driving or on-duty time in the middle means you do not yet have 10 consecutive hours off. A valid split-sleeper pair is a separate, specific option, not a pair of random naps.

questions.q: Nine consecutive hours off duty are finished and the driver feels alert. May this property-carrying driver start driving?
options: No. Nine hours is short of the required 10 consecutive hours off duty
Yes. Nine hours resets the 11 and the 14 whenever the driver signs the log
Yes. Alertness replaces the tenth hour
Yes. A 30-minute break on top of 9 hours equals a 10-hour reset
questions.explanation: The reset is 10 consecutive hours off duty, not 9. Feeling alert does not shorten it, and a 30-minute break is not the missing hour that restarts the 11 and the 14.

questions.q: Thirty-four consecutive hours off duty are used by a property-carrying driver for what purpose?
options: To replace the ELD with a paper grid for the next week
To restart the 60-hour or 70-hour on-duty clock
To extend today's 14-hour window by 34 hours
To erase the 30-minute break requirement for the next month
questions.explanation: A 34-hour restart applies to the weekly 60/70 calculation. It does not hand you extra driving time inside a 14-hour window, and it is not a logging shortcut.

questions.q: Can 34 hours off duty be split into a 20-hour piece and a later 14-hour piece and still restart the weekly clock?
options: Yes, if both pieces are logged as on-duty not driving
Yes. Twenty hours is the restart by itself
No. The 34 hours must be consecutive
Yes. Any 34 off-duty hours in an 8-day span restart the 70
questions.explanation: The weekly restart is 34 consecutive hours off duty. A gap of on-duty or driving time breaks the streak, and a shorter total does not restart the 60/70 clock.

questions.q: Thirty-three consecutive hours off duty are complete. Has the property-carrying driver restarted the 60/70-hour clock?
options: Yes. Anything over 24 hours restarts the weekly total
Yes. Thirty-three hours also adds 33 hours to the 14-hour window
Yes, but only if the carrier does not operate every day
No. The restart is 34 consecutive hours, so 33 is not enough
questions.explanation: Do not round 33 up to 34. Until 34 consecutive hours off duty are finished, the 60/70-hour total is still in force.

questions.q: During an ongoing 14-hour window the driver considers starting a 34-hour break early to gain extra driving time tonight. What would that 34-hour period actually do?
options: It would not add extra hours inside the current 14-hour window
It would immediately grant 2 more driving hours tonight
It would pause the 14 and let the driver finish the old window next week
It would convert the remaining 3 driving hours into 34 driving hours
questions.explanation: You cannot use a 34-hour restart as a booster inside today's 14. The 14 still ends on its own clock. The 34 matters to the 60/70 total, and only if it is consecutive time off duty.

questions.q: A property-carrying driver is ill and still has 5 hours left on the 11-hour clock inside the 14-hour window. What is the duty?
options: Drive until midnight, when both clocks reset
Do not drive
Drive the 5 hours slowly
Drive if a 20-minute break is taken first
questions.explanation: 49 CFR 392.3 says you may not drive while your ability is impaired by illness or fatigue. Time left on the 11 or the 14 does not override that. Illness or fatigue bars driving even when the clocks still have time.
questions.remember: Too tired or sick? Don't drive.

questions.q: The driver's eyes are closing, but 2 driving hours remain and the 14-hour window has not ended. What should a property-carrying driver do?
options: Take a 4-hour nap and treat it as a full reset of the 11 and the 14
Switch the log to off duty while continuing to drive
Stop driving. Fatigue prohibits driving even with hours left on both daily clocks
Finish the 2 hours
questions.explanation: Being sleepy is a reason to stop, not a reason to push the last hours. A 4-hour nap does not reset the daily clocks, and logging off duty while driving is a false log.
questions.remember: Too tired or sick? Don't drive.

questions.q: A dispatcher says the freight must move and the driver is too sick to drive safely, though the 14-hour window is still open. Who is right?
options: The dispatcher, because on-duty orders suspend the illness rule
The driver may drive if the ELD still shows driving time
The driver may drive for 2 extra hours under the adverse-conditions idea of being sick
The driver must not drive while ill, and carrier pressure does not create hours the body can use
questions.explanation: Illness is not an adverse driving condition and it is not cured by a dispatch order. If you cannot drive safely, you do not drive, even when 395.3 still shows time.
questions.remember: Too tired or sick? Don't drive.

questions.q: A 4-hour nap in the sleeper is the only rest this property-carrying driver has taken since coming on duty. Does it reset the 11 and the 14?
options: No. A 4-hour nap is not 10 consecutive hours off and is not a valid split-sleeper pair
Yes. Any sleeper-berth period of at least 2 hours resets both daily clocks
Yes. Four hours is the modern replacement for the 10-hour break
It resets the 60/70-hour clock but not the daily clocks
questions.explanation: Do not treat a nap as a reset. The daily clocks need 10 consecutive hours off duty, or a valid split pair of at least 7 consecutive sleeper hours plus a separate period of at least 2 hours off duty or in the sleeper, together at least 10 hours.
questions.remember: Sleeper split: at least 7 in the berth.

questions.q: Which split-sleeper pair can qualify for a property-carrying driver?
options: Seven hours off duty in a chair and no time in the sleeper berth
7+ hours in the sleeper plus 2+ hours, totaling 10
Any 8 hours in the sleeper paired with any 2 hours on duty not driving
A single 4-hour nap
questions.explanation: Both pieces have minimums, and the total must reach 10 hours. The long piece has to be in the sleeper. The short piece has to be off duty or in the sleeper, not on-duty not driving. A lone nap is not a pair. At least 7 consecutive hours in the sleeper berth, plus a separate period of at least 2 consecutive hours off duty or in the sleeper, together totaling at least 10 hours.
questions.remember: Sleeper split: at least 7 in the berth.

questions.q: Seven consecutive hours in the sleeper are paired with a separate 2 consecutive hours off duty. Why does that pair fail?
options: It fails because the short period was off duty instead of on duty not driving
It succeeds, and it also restarts the 70-hour clock
Together they are only 9 hours, and the two periods must total at least 10 hours
It fails because 8 and 2 is the only legal split
questions.explanation: Each piece can meet its own minimum and the pair can still fail the total. Seven plus 2 is 9, which is short of 10. The pair also does not restart the 60/70-hour clock.
questions.remember: Sleeper split: the two add up to 10.

questions.q: Seven consecutive sleeper-berth hours are paired with a separate 3 consecutive hours off duty. How should a property-carrying driver treat that pair?
options: It is invalid because the long period must be exactly 8 hours and the short period exactly 2
It resets the 11 and the 14 and also zeroes the 60/70-hour total
It is invalid because off-duty time can never be the shorter period
It can be a valid split, and when the pair is valid those two periods do not count against the 14-hour window
questions.explanation: Seven in the sleeper and 3 off duty meet the minimums and total 10. A valid pair's two periods do not count against the 14-hour window. Eight-and-two is one possible pattern, not the only one. The weekly clock is a separate rule.
questions.remember: Qualifying split rest pauses the 14-hour window.

questions.q: Eight consecutive hours in the sleeper plus a separate 2 hours off duty total 10. Is that the only legal split for property-carrying drivers?
options: No. Seven plus three, among others, also works
Yes. Eight and 2 replaced every other combination
No, because eight and 2 is now illegal and only a 4-hour nap works
Yes, and that pair also restarts the 34-hour weekly calculation by itself
questions.explanation: Do not teach 8-and-2 as the only split. It can be valid when the periods and the 10-hour total are met. A 7-hour sleeper period paired with a separate qualifying period that makes the total at least 10 is also the property-carrying rule. No. Eight and 2 can qualify, but it is not the only pattern. Seven sleeper hours plus enough additional off-duty or sleeper time to reach 10 also can.
questions.remember: Sleeper split: at least 7 in the berth.

questions.q: The long rest was 7 hours off duty in the passenger seat, not in the sleeper, plus 3 hours in the sleeper. Does that split work?
options: Yes. It also removes those 10 hours from the 60/70 total by restarting it
No. The period of at least 7 consecutive hours must be in the sleeper berth
Yes. Off duty and sleeper berth are interchangeable for the 7-hour piece
Yes. Three hours in the sleeper upgrades any shorter rest into a 10-hour reset
questions.explanation: The 7-hour piece is sleeper-berth time specifically. Off duty can be used for the separate period of at least 2 hours, but it cannot replace the 7 hours in the berth.
questions.remember: Sleeper split: at least 7 in the berth.

questions.q: Eight hours in the sleeper are paired with 2 hours on duty not driving, spent fueling and watching the dock. Is that a valid property-carrying split?
options: Yes. Any 2 hours that are not driving complete an 8-and-2 split
Yes. Those 2 hours also extend the 14-hour window by 2 hours automatically
No. The shorter period must be at least 2 consecutive hours off duty or in the sleeper, not on-duty not driving
Yes. On-duty not driving counts as the 2-hour piece because it counts as the 30-minute break
questions.explanation: The 30-minute break may be on-duty not driving. The split-sleeper short period may not. It has to be off duty or in the sleeper, and the pair still has to total at least 10 hours.
questions.remember: Short split period: off duty or berth.

questions.q: When a property-carrying split-sleeper pair is valid, what happens to those two periods in the 14-hour calculation?
options: They extend the 14-hour window by 34 hours
They erase driving time already used on the 11-hour clock
They restart the 60/70-hour clock the same way 34 hours off duty would
They do not count against the 14-hour window
questions.explanation: A valid pair is the specific case in which those two rest periods are excluded from the 14-hour window. That is not true of an ordinary nap, and it is not a weekly restart.
questions.remember: Qualifying split rest pauses the 14-hour window.

questions.q: An ordinary 45-minute off-duty lunch sits in the middle of the duty day and is not part of a split pair. Does the 14-hour window pause?
options: No. Ordinary off-duty time inside the day does not extend the 14-hour clock
Yes. Lunch is excluded from the 14 the same way a valid split pair is
Yes. Any off-duty period of at least 30 minutes pauses the 14
Yes. The pause equals the lunch plus the next 2 hours
questions.explanation: Do not confuse the 30-minute driving break, or lunch, with a valid split. Ordinary breaks do not stop the 14. Only the two periods of a valid split are kept out of that window.

questions.q: Unexpected adverse conditions that actually meet the exception can change a property-carrying driver's day by how much?
options: Nothing. Adverse weather never affects either daily limit
Up to 2 extra hours of driving, and the 14-hour window may be extended by up to 2 hours
Up to 4 extra driving hours and a new 34-hour weekly restart
A full reset of the 11 and the 14, as if 10 hours off had been taken
questions.explanation: The adverse-driving-conditions exception, when its conditions are truly met, can allow up to 2 additional driving hours and can extend the 14-hour window by up to 2 hours. It is not a new 10-hour break.
questions.remember: Adverse conditions: up to 2 extra hours.

questions.q: The driver left the dock an hour late and then met heavier traffic than hoped. May the adverse-driving-conditions exception be used?
options: Yes. Late dispatch automatically extends both the 11 and the 70-hour clock
Yes. Heavier traffic lets you skip the 30-minute break for the rest of the week
No. Starting late, or traffic that is merely heavier than you hoped, does not meet the exception
Yes. Any delay the driver did not enjoy qualifies for 2 extra hours
questions.explanation: The exception is not a cushion for a late start or for ordinary congestion. Use it only when the exception's conditions are actually met, and even then it is limited to up to 2 hours, not a weekly reset.

questions.q: Adverse conditions that qualify have already been used for 2 extra driving hours. Can they also restart the 60/70-hour clock?
options: Yes. Two adverse hours wipe the 8-day total clean
Yes, if the weather lasts until midnight
Yes. Adverse conditions replace the 34-hour restart
No. The exception does not restart the weekly on-duty limit
questions.explanation: Up to 2 extra driving hours and up to 2 hours on the 14-hour window are the adverse-conditions relief when the rule applies. The 60/70-hour limit still applies.
questions.remember: Adverse conditions: up to 2 extra hours.

questions.q: The clock passes midnight while a property-carrying driver is still inside the same 14-hour window. What resets?
options: Nothing about the 11-hour or 14-hour clocks
Both the 11 and the 14 reset
Only the 11 resets
The 70-hour clock resets, and so does the 30-minute break
questions.explanation: Duty limits are not calendar-day limits. Crossing midnight does not give you a fresh 11 or a fresh 14. You still need a qualifying 10-hour break or a valid split. A new calendar day does not reset them.

questions.q: Passenger-carrying drivers are different from property-carrying drivers. If you are assigned a bus, which daily limits do you follow?
options: Eleven hours of driving inside a 15-hour window
The passenger-carrying limits, including 10 hours of driving and a 15-hour limit
The property-carrying 11-hour driving limit and 14-hour window
Whichever pair of numbers gives more driving time that day
questions.explanation: Do not apply the property-carrying rule to a passenger-carrying assignment. Passenger-carrying drivers use their own limits: 10 hours of driving and a 15-hour limit. Freight drivers do not borrow those numbers.

questions.q: A property-carrying dispatcher tells you to use the bus limits of 10 driving hours and a 15-hour window for this trailer. What should you do?
options: Use 10 hours of driving inside a 14-hour window
Use 11 hours of driving inside a 15-hour window
Refuse that mix
Use 10 and 15
questions.explanation: Passenger-carrying drivers are different, and their rule is for that work. A property-carrying driver uses 11 hours of driving after 10 consecutive hours off, inside a 14-hour window. Do not swap the two.

questions.q: This freight trip is only 40 miles. May the property-carrying driver ignore the 11-hour and 14-hour limits because a short-haul exception exists somewhere in the rules?
options: Yes. Any trip under 50 miles drops both daily limits
Yes. Short trips use the passenger-carrying 15-hour window
Yes. The 11-hour limit is only for trips over 500 miles
No. Every condition of an exception must be met
questions.explanation: Do not treat a short trip as an automatic exemption. The normal property-carrying limits remain unless every condition of a specific exception is actually met.
questions.remember: Short-haul: every condition, or no exception.

questions.q: A coworker says the short-haul exception erases the need to obey 395.3 whenever the driver gets home the same day. What is the accurate reply?
options: The normal 11-hour and 14-hour limits still apply unless every condition of the exception is met
Same-day return always replaces the 14-hour window with unlimited on-duty time
Same-day return resets the 60/70-hour clock at the driveway
The exception is the normal rule for every property-carrying driver
questions.explanation: Mentioning that an exception exists is not the same as meeting it. Unless every required condition is true, the property-carrying driver stays on the 11, the 14, the 30-minute break, and the 60/70. Getting home is not itself the exception.
questions.remember: Short-haul: every condition, or no exception.

questions.q: Most property-carrying drivers who must record duty status are required to use an ELD. If you are one of them, may a handwritten notebook replace it?
options: Yes, if you copy the paper into the ELD at the end of the week
No. If an ELD is required, paper wishful thinking does not replace it
Yes. Paper is always equal to an ELD if the handwriting is neat
Yes, whenever the truck stays inside one state
questions.explanation: An ELD is required for most drivers who must keep a record of duty status. Do not invent an exemption. If you are required to use an ELD, a paper log does not take its place.
questions.remember: Most drivers log with an ELD.

questions.q: You are required to use an ELD and you edit it so two hours of driving appear as off duty. What is that record?
options: A valid split-sleeper entry, even though you were driving
A 34-hour restart recorded in advance
A false log that hides real driving
A legal reconstruction
questions.explanation: The log has to match the truth. Changing driving time to off duty, sleeper, or on-duty not driving to conceal it is a false log, whether you do it on paper or in the ELD. A false log. Editing a record to hide driving is not a correction of a real error.

questions.q: While driving, the property-carrying driver sets the duty status to sleeper berth so the 14-hour clock looks shorter. What rules does that break?
options: It is allowed once per day as a personal-use edit
It converts the driving into the 7-hour half of a split sleeper
It is legal if the passenger seat is empty
It falsifies the log; the clocks keep running
questions.explanation: Duty status has to be what you are actually doing. Calling driving time sleeper berth hides hours and does not change the fact that you were driving inside the 11 and the 14. It creates a false log, and it does not actually stop the real 14-hour window or the 11-hour driving count.

questions.q: Six hours of driving, then 3 hours on duty not driving at the dock, then 2 more hours of driving. How much of the 11-hour driving limit is used?
options: Eight hours; only driving counts toward the 11
Eleven hours, because all on-duty time is driving time
Five hours, because the dock time is subtracted from driving
Two hours, because only the last driving segment counts after a dock stop
questions.explanation: Add the driving segments: 6 plus 2 is 8 hours toward the 11. On-duty not driving does not add to the 11 and does not erase driving already done. It does consume the 14-hour window and the 60/70 total. Eight hours. Only the driving counts against the 11. The 3 dock hours still count on the 14 and the weekly limit.

questions.q: The same dock stop of 3 hours on duty not driving happens before any driving. The 11-hour driving allowance at that moment is still what?
options: Zero, until a new 10-hour break is taken after loading
Still 11, limited by what fits in the 14
Eight hours, because the dock time is deducted from the 11
Fourteen hours of driving
questions.explanation: Loading does not spend the 11-hour driving limit. It does spend the 14-hour window. If the window now has fewer than 11 hours left, you cannot use the full 11. Still 11 hours of driving available, but only the hours that will fit before the 14th hour.

questions.q: On-duty time in the last 7 days is 60 hours, and this carrier does not operate every day. The 11 and the 14 still show time. May the property-carrying driver drive?
options: Yes, after a 30-minute break, which resets the 60
Yes, after 10 consecutive hours off, which always clears the 60
No. The 60-hour limit in 7 days has been reached, so driving is not allowed
Yes. Daily clocks outrank the weekly total
questions.explanation: You may not drive after 60 on-duty hours in 7 consecutive days when that is the carrier's rule. Ten hours off resets the 11 and the 14 only. It does not, by itself, reset the 60.
questions.remember: Not every day: 60 hours in 7 days.

questions.q: This every-day carrier's driver has 70 on-duty hours in the last 8 days and a full 11-hour driving balance after 10 hours off. What blocks the trip?
options: Nothing. Ten hours off resets the 70 as well as the 11 and the 14
Only fatigue, because 70 hours is advisory
The 30-minute break, which must be taken before the first mile even with zero driving today
The 70-hour limit in 8 days
questions.explanation: Weekly and daily limits both apply. Ten consecutive hours off starts a new 11 and 14, but the 70-hour total remains until hours drop out of the 8-day window or a 34-hour restart is completed.

questions.q: Which kinds of time count toward the 60-hour or 70-hour on-duty limit?
options: Driving and on-duty not driving
Only driving time
Every hour on the calendar, including a 34-hour restart
Only sleeper-berth time
questions.explanation: The weekly cap is an on-duty cap. Count driving and other on-duty work. Do not count off duty or sleeper berth as on-duty hours. A 34-hour restart is consecutive off-duty time, not on-duty time.
questions.remember: On duty: all work time, not only driving.

questions.q: A 30-minute break is taken after the weekly on-duty total is already at the 60-hour limit. What changes?
options: The break extends the 14-hour window by 30 minutes and clears the weekly cap
Nothing about the weekly limit
The 60-hour total drops by 30 minutes and driving may resume
The break restarts both the 7-day and 8-day calculations
questions.explanation: The 30-minute break only interrupts driving after 8 hours of driving time. It is not a weekly restart and it does not give back on-duty hours already accumulated.
questions.remember: A break does not reset the weekly limit.

questions.q: After a valid 30-minute break, 3 hours remain on the 11-hour clock and 4 hours remain in the 14-hour window. How much more may this fit property-carrying driver drive?
options: Eight hours, because the break restored a full driving block
Eleven hours, because the break reset the driving clock
Three hours; the 11-hour balance is tighter
Four hours, because the 14 is the only limit that matters after a break
questions.explanation: Use the remaining 11 and the remaining 14, and stop at the smaller one. The break did not put hours back on either clock. Here the 11 runs out first, at 3 hours. Three hours, because the 11-hour balance is the tighter limit and the break did not add driving time.

questions.q: After a valid 30-minute break, 3 driving hours remain on the 11, but only 2 hours remain before the 14th hour. How much more driving is legal?
options: Three hours, because the 11-hour balance ignores the 14
Five hours, by adding the two remainders together
Two hours plus a 20-minute extension for the break just taken
Two hours; the 14-hour window ends first
questions.explanation: Both limits apply at once. You must stop driving when the first one runs out. Two hours of window means two hours of driving, even though the 11-hour clock shows 3.

questions.q: The 14-hour window ended at 8 p.m. A 30-minute break is finished at 8:10 p.m. May the property-carrying driver start driving again that night?
options: No. The break does not reopen the window
Yes. Any 30-minute break starts a new 14-hour window
Yes, for the driving hours that were still on the 11
Yes, until midnight, when the window resets anyway
questions.explanation: Once 14 hours have passed since the end of the last qualifying 10-hour break, you may not drive. A short break does not start the clock over. You need 10 consecutive hours off, or a valid split pair. No. The 30-minute break does not reopen a 14-hour window that has already ended.

questions.q: Driving time today is 8 hours and the driver has not yet taken 30 consecutive minutes off the driving seat. What must happen before more driving?
options: Two 10-minute stretches that add up to 20 minutes
A break of at least 30 consecutive minutes
Nothing, until 11 driving hours are complete
A full 10-hour off-duty period before another mile
questions.explanation: Eight cumulative hours of driving, not of all on-duty time, is the trigger. The next driving has to wait for 30 consecutive minutes that are not driving. That break still does not reset the 11 or the 14.

questions.q: The driver has been on duty not driving for 8 hours and has not driven at all today. Is the 30-minute break already required?
options: Yes. On-duty not driving counts one-for-one as driving toward the 8
Yes, and those 8 hours have also used up the 11-hour driving limit
No. The break is tied to 8 cumulative hours of driving, not to 8 hours of all on-duty time
Yes. Any 8 on-duty hours require the break before the ignition is used
questions.explanation: Do not mix the clocks. On-duty not driving consumes the 14-hour window and the weekly limit. The 30-minute rule waits for 8 hours of actual driving.

questions.q: Sleeper-berth time of 40 consecutive minutes follows 8 hours of driving. Can that be the required break for a property-carrying driver?
options: No. The sleeper only counts if the period is at least 7 hours
Yes. Forty minutes in the sleeper also restarts the 14-hour window
No. The break must be on-duty not driving and cannot be sleeper time
Yes, without resetting the 11 or the 14
questions.explanation: Off duty, sleeper berth, or on-duty not driving can all be the 30-minute interruption. A short sleeper period is not, by itself, a split-sleeper reset of the daily clocks.

questions.q: Twenty-five consecutive minutes off duty follow 8 hours of driving. Why is the property-carrying driver still not free to drive?
options: The break must be at least 30 consecutive minutes, so 25 is short
Twenty-five minutes is enough if it is logged as sleeper berth instead
Twenty-five minutes resets the 11-hour clock even though it misses the 30
The driver may drive
questions.explanation: Do not round a short break up to 30 minutes. Finish at least 30 consecutive minutes before you drive again. Those minutes do not extend the 14.

questions.q: Two employers used this property-carrying driver today. How do the 11-hour and 14-hour limits apply?
options: The driver may choose the carrier with the larger remaining weekly total and ignore the other
They follow the driver
Each carrier gets its own 11 hours and its own 14-hour window
Only the first carrier's hours count, and the second job is off the log
questions.explanation: 395.3 applies regardless of the number of motor carriers using the driver. You cannot reset the day by changing companies, and you cannot hide the first carrier's driving. Hours for both carriers count together, and a second company does not start a fresh clock.

questions.q: The co-driver is rested, but your own 14-hour window is over. May you drive the next leg because the team still has a fresh driver on paper?
options: Yes, if you log the leg on the co-driver's ELD
Yes. Team drivers are exempt from the 14-hour window
No. Your clocks are your own
Yes. Team operations pool the 11-hour limit between the two drivers
questions.explanation: Each driver complies individually. Logging your driving on someone else's record would be a false log. If your window is closed, you do not drive. No. Your clocks are yours. Another driver's available hours do not reset your 11 or your 14.

questions.q: A qualifying 10 consecutive hours off duty was spent entirely in the sleeper berth. What daily clocks can start again for this property-carrying driver?
options: Only the 30-minute break
The 60/70-hour clock, but not the 11 or the 14
Nothing, unless the berth time was also a 34-hour restart
The 11-hour and 14-hour clocks
questions.explanation: Ten consecutive hours of rest in the sleeper berth satisfies the 10 consecutive hours off duty that restart the 11 and the 14. Weekly hours are unchanged unless the rest was a full 34-hour restart.
questions.remember: 10 straight hours in the berth counts.

questions.q: You have 3 driving hours left and you are already at the 14th hour. A 4-hour sleeper nap is the plan before you finish those 3 hours. Will that nap both pause the problem and reset the day?
options: No. A 4-hour nap resets neither clock
Yes. Four sleeper hours reopen the 14 and preserve the 3 driving hours
Yes. Any nap at the 14th hour becomes a 34-hour restart
Yes, if the 4 hours are logged as on-duty not driving
questions.explanation: The user's situation is the closed window: leftover driving time cannot be used after the 14th hour. A 4-hour nap is neither 10 consecutive hours off nor a valid split pair, so it does not restart those clocks.
questions.remember: A short nap is not a valid split.

questions.q: Which rest actually lets a property-carrying driver begin a new 11-hour driving period and a new 14-hour window?
options: Eight hours off duty if the carrier operates every day
Ten hours off, or a valid split-sleeper pair
Any sleeper period of at least 4 hours
A 30-minute break plus midnight
questions.explanation: The normal reset is 10 consecutive hours off duty. The split alternative is specific: at least 7 consecutive hours in the sleeper, a separate period of at least 2 consecutive hours off duty or in the sleeper, together at least 10, and when valid those periods do not count against the 14.
questions.remember: Sleeper split: the two add up to 10.

questions.q: A valid split has just been completed. The 60/70-hour total was already high. Did the split clear the weekly clock?
options: Yes, if one of the periods was at least 7 hours
Yes. The short 2-hour period is what restarts the 70
No. Only 34 hours off restarts the 60/70
Yes. Any split that fixes the 14 also zeroes the weekly total
questions.explanation: Keep the resets separate. The split changes how the 14-hour window is calculated. The weekly on-duty total moves only when time drops out of the 7 or 8 days, or when 34 consecutive hours off duty restart it.

questions.q: On-duty hours are 58 in 7 days for a carrier that does not run every day. Tomorrow's plan would add 6 on-duty hours, including driving. What limit hits first?
options: No weekly problem
The 70-hour rule
None, if the 6 hours include a 30-minute break that subtracts from the 60
The 60-hour limit in 7 days
questions.explanation: This carrier's drivers use 60 hours in 7 days, not 70 in 8. On-duty time, including driving, has 2 hours of room left. A 30-minute break does not subtract from the weekly total. Only 2 more on-duty hours fit, even if the 11 and the 14 would allow more driving.
questions.remember: Not every day: 60 hours in 7 days.

questions.q: An every-day carrier shows 66 on-duty hours in the current 8-day period. How much on-duty time remains under the property-carrying weekly rule?
options: Four hours, because the limit is 70 in 8 consecutive days
Fourteen hours, because a new 14-hour window replaces the 70
Ten hours, because a 10-hour break will be subtracted from the 66
Zero, because 60 in 7 days always applies on top and 66 is already over 60
questions.explanation: When the carrier operates every day, 70 hours in 8 days is the weekly limit. Sixty-six leaves 4 on-duty hours. Do not also impose the 60-in-7 rule on that carrier as if it were the tighter daily company rule.

questions.q: Which statement keeps the adverse-driving-conditions exception inside its real size?
options: It applies whenever the driver started the trip late
Up to 2 extra hours, only when conditions are met
It adds 2 hours to the 11, the 14, and the 70 every time traffic is slow
It replaces the 10-hour break after any weather delay
questions.explanation: Do not widen the exception. Late starts and traffic that is only heavier than you hoped do not qualify. When the conditions are truly met, the relief is up to 2 hours, not a new weekly restart. It can add up to 2 driving hours and extend the 14-hour window by up to 2 hours, and only when the exception's conditions are actually met.
questions.remember: Adverse conditions: up to 2 extra hours.

questions.q: Snow was forecast before the trip and the driver left late anyway. The road is now merely busy. Why is the 2-hour adverse exception unavailable?
options: Leaving late is itself the adverse condition and grants 2 hours plus a 34-hour restart
Busy roads extend the 14-hour window by the length of the delay with no cap
Known or ordinary delays do not qualify
Snow never relates to adverse conditions
questions.explanation: Use the exception only when its conditions are actually met. A delay you created by starting late, or ordinary heavier traffic, is not that exception. Do not take the 2 hours on that story.

questions.q: The ELD malfunctions and you are required to use one. What is the wrong response?
options: Following the required malfunction steps and not hiding driving time
Keeping an accurate record of the driving that actually occurred
Refusing to invent off-duty time for miles you drove
Using a notebook and erasing the missed driving
questions.explanation: A malfunction is not permission to conceal hours. If an ELD is required, paper wishful thinking does not replace it, and editing the record to hide driving is a false log. Switching to a private notebook and later editing the record so the missing driving never appears.

questions.q: Which edit is a false log for a driver who must use an ELD?
options: Changing a driving segment to off duty so the 11-hour total looks smaller
Adding a remark that describes a real traffic stop
Certifying a record that matches the driving you actually did
Showing on-duty not driving for a real loading period when you were not driving
questions.explanation: The record has to show driving as driving. Shrinking the 11-hour total by relabeling driving is a false log. True on-duty not driving, such as real loading, is supposed to be logged as itself.

questions.q: You do not know whether some ELD exemption covers this truck. What is the safe course that does not invent an exemption list?
options: Log the trip as off duty until someone proves an exemption does not apply
Use the ELD unless you truly meet every condition of an exemption
Drop the ELD
Keep two logs and submit the one with fewer driving hours
questions.explanation: Most drivers who must record duty status must use an ELD. Exemptions are real only when every condition is met. Guessing at the list, or hiding driving, is not compliance. Do not switch to paper just because an exemption might exist.
questions.remember: Most drivers log with an ELD.

questions.q: A property-carrying driver drove 11 hours, took 10 consecutive hours off, and the weekly total is still under the cap. What may the new duty period include?
options: Fourteen extra weekly hours added on top of the old 60 or 70
No driving, because 10 hours off is only a 30-minute break
A new 11-hour driving limit and a new 14-hour window
A new 14 hours of driving
questions.explanation: Ten consecutive hours off duty refreshes the 11 and the 14 only. Keep counting on-duty time toward 60 in 7 days or 70 in 8 days, whichever applies to the carrier. The weekly total did not reset.

questions.q: Halfway through a 34-hour off-duty restart the driver goes on duty for an hour to move the truck in the yard, then parks again. Is the restart still intact?
options: Yes. Yard moves under an hour are ignored inside a restart
Yes. The restart becomes a 14-hour extension instead
Yes, if the yard move is logged as sleeper berth
No. The 34 hours must be consecutive
questions.explanation: Consecutive means consecutive. On-duty work in the middle, including a yard move you are on duty to perform, breaks the 34 hours. Logging it as sleeper while you work would also be a false log.

questions.q: Which property-carrying total is an on-duty total rather than a driving-only total?
options: The 60-hour or 70-hour on-duty limit
The 11-hour limit, which includes every loading hour
The 30-minute break
The 14-hour window, which counts only driving minutes
questions.explanation: The 11 counts driving. The 30-minute rule waits on driving time. The 14 is a consecutive-hour window that includes everything after you come on duty. The 60/70 counts all on-duty time, driving or not.
questions.remember: The 60 and 70-hour limits count all on-duty time.

questions.q: Came on duty at 7 a.m. after 10 consecutive hours off. It is now 9 p.m. How should the 14-hour rule be applied?
options: Drive, because 9 p.m. is before midnight and midnight resets the window
Do not drive
Drive until 11 p.m.
Drive if the odometer shows fewer than 11 hours of driving
questions.explanation: Seven a.m. plus 14 hours is 9 p.m. After that hour you may not drive. Leftover time on the 11-hour clock does not extend the window, and midnight does not reset it. Fourteen hours have passed since that qualifying break ended, even if driving time remains.

questions.q: Came on duty at 7 a.m. The driver was off duty, not in a valid split, from 11 a.m. to 1 p.m. When does the 14-hour window end?
options: At 1 p.m. the next day
At midnight, regardless of when the driver came on duty
At 9 p.m. The two off-duty hours did not extend the window
At 11 p.m., because the two hours are added to the 14
questions.explanation: Ordinary off-duty time inside the day does not pause the 14. The window still ends 14 hours after the qualifying 10-hour break ended and the driver came on duty, which here is 9 p.m.

questions.q: A 20-minute off-duty coffee stop is the only interruption after 8 hours 10 minutes of driving. May the property-carrying driver leave the lot?
options: Yes. The extra 10 minutes of driving cancel the need for a break
Yes. Coffee stops extend the 14-hour window by the same 20 minutes
Yes. Any stop after 8 hours resets the 11-hour driving limit
No. The break must be 30 consecutive minutes
questions.explanation: Once 8 cumulative hours of driving have been reached, get at least 30 consecutive minutes before you drive again. The 20-minute stop fails that test and does not move the 14. No. Twenty minutes is not the required 30 consecutive minutes, and those 8 driving hours already require the break before more driving.

questions.q: Loading kept the driver on duty not driving from 6 a.m. to 10 a.m. Driving then starts. Which description of the remaining day is right?
options: The 11 is intact, but only 10 hours fit in the 14
The 11-hour limit has fallen to 7 hours and the 14-hour window starts fresh at 10 a.m.
Both clocks start at 10 a.m., giving 11 driving hours inside a new 14
The loading hours paused the 14, so 14 driving hours remain
questions.explanation: On-duty loading from 6 to 10 consumed 4 hours of the 14 and none of the 11. The window ends at 8 p.m., which leaves 10 hours. You cannot drive 11 hours inside a window that has only 10 hours left. The 11-hour driving limit is still intact, but the 14-hour window already has only 10 hours left, so at most 10 of those driving hours can be used.

questions.q: Which pairing shows a property-carrying split done wrong, the way a 4-hour nap is done wrong?
options: Ten consecutive hours off duty with no split at all
Four consecutive sleeper hours alone, offered as if they reset the 11-hour and 14-hour clocks
Seven consecutive sleeper hours plus a separate 3 consecutive hours off duty, together 10
Eight consecutive sleeper hours plus a separate 2 consecutive hours off duty, together 10
questions.explanation: A 4-hour nap does not meet the 7-hour sleeper piece, does not total 10 hours with a qualifying partner period, and does not reset the daily clocks. The other patterns are real qualifying rests.
questions.remember: Sleeper split: at least 7 in the berth.

questions.q: Seven consecutive hours in the sleeper plus a separate 4 consecutive hours off duty total more than 10. Is the extra hour a problem?
options: Yes. Anything over 8 and 2 is the old illegal pattern
Yes. The extra hour restarts the 70-hour clock whether you want it or not
No. The rules set minimums, not exact totals
Yes. The total must be exactly 10, so the extra hour voids the split
questions.explanation: At least 7 in the sleeper, at least 2 more off duty or in the sleeper, together at least 10. A longer short period is fine. The pair still does not, by itself, restart the 60/70-hour clock. No. The rules set minimums, including a total of at least 10. More than 10 is still valid if the 7 and the separate 2-hour minimums are met.
questions.remember: Sleeper split: the two add up to 10.

questions.q: The shorter split period is 2 consecutive hours in the sleeper, and the other period is 8 consecutive hours in the sleeper. Can both periods be sleeper berth?
options: No. One period must be on-duty not driving
No. The rules allow only one sleeper period per week
No. Two sleeper periods always count in full against the 14 even when the pair is valid
Yes. The 2-hour period may be in the sleeper
questions.explanation: Both pieces may be in the sleeper. The long piece has to be. The short piece is allowed to be. When the pair is valid, those two periods do not count against the 14-hour window. Yes. The period of at least 2 hours may be off duty or in the sleeper, and the 7-or-more hours must be in the sleeper. Together these total more than 10.
questions.remember: Short split period: off duty or berth.

questions.q: A driver claims a personal nap of any length resets the 14-hour window. What is the correction?
options: No nap by itself resets that window
Any nap of at least 30 minutes resets the 14 but not the 11
Naps reset the window only at midnight
Naps reset the window only for passenger-carrying drivers using the property rule
questions.explanation: Ordinary rest inside the day does not extend the 14. The split rule is narrow, and a short nap is not a qualifying pair. Do not teach that any sleeper time restarts the clock. You need 10 consecutive hours off duty or a valid split pair, and a 4-hour nap is neither.
questions.remember: Qualifying split rest pauses the 14-hour window.

questions.q: Which hours may be excluded from the 14-hour window for a property-carrying driver?
options: The two hours granted for a late dispatch
The two periods of a valid split pair
Every off-duty minute of the day
Every on-duty not driving minute
questions.explanation: Valid split periods do not count against the 14. Ordinary breaks do. A late start is not an adverse-conditions grant. On-duty not driving stays inside the 14 and the weekly total. The two periods of a valid split-sleeper pair, and not an ordinary 20-minute or 4-hour nap.
questions.remember: Qualifying split rest pauses the 14-hour window.

questions.q: The weekly calculation is a rolling period of consecutive days, not a calendar week that clears on Sunday night. What does that mean at the end of Sunday?
options: Only the 11-hour clock resets at Sunday midnight
A 30-minute break taken on Sunday night is the weekly restart
Sunday night does not zero the 60/70 total
The 60 and the 70 both reset at midnight every Sunday
questions.explanation: The limits are any 7 consecutive days or any 8 consecutive days, depending on the carrier. Midnight, including a weekend midnight, does not reset the 11, the 14, or the weekly total. Hours still count until they fall outside the 7 or 8 consecutive days, or a 34-hour restart is completed.

questions.q: A 34-hour restart ends Monday at 6 a.m. The driver comes on duty then. What daily limits are available, and what is not added?
options: Thirty-four extra driving hours to be used before the new 14 starts
A 15-hour passenger window
Only 8 driving hours
A new 11-hour driving limit and a new 14-hour window
