questions.explanation: Thirty-four consecutive hours off duty restarts the 60/70 calculation and, because it includes a 10-hour break, a new daily period can start. It does not inflate a 14-hour window. The 34 hours do not add extra driving time inside some older 14-hour window.

questions.q: You are under both the 11 and the 14, but you are too fatigued to control the truck. Which rule decides?
options: Do not drive
Drive. The 11 and the 14 are the only limits that can stop a trip
Drive for 2 adverse-condition hours
Take a 20-minute break and the fatigue rule no longer applies
questions.explanation: Clocks are maximums, not a requirement to keep driving. If illness or fatigue impairs you, stop. A short break does not cancel that duty. The illness and fatigue prohibition applies even when 395.3 still shows time.
questions.remember: Too tired or sick? Don't drive.

questions.q: Which cargo-free statement about the 14-hour window is accurate for property-carrying drivers?
options: The window applies only to passenger-carrying drivers
No driving after the 14th hour, even with time left
You may drive all 14 hours, and off-duty breaks add more hours on the end
The window pauses for every on-duty activity that is not driving
questions.explanation: The 14 is a consecutive limit on when you may drive, not a promise of 14 driving hours. Ordinary breaks do not extend it. Property-carrying drivers use this window, not the passenger rule. You may not drive after the 14th hour from the end of the last qualifying 10-hour break, even when driving time remains.

questions.q: Which driving total is the property-carrying maximum after 10 consecutive hours off duty?
options: Fourteen hours of driving inside a 15-hour window
Eight hours of driving before a mandatory 10-hour break
Eleven hours of driving
Ten hours of driving, the same number used for passenger-carrying drivers
questions.explanation: Remember the property numbers: 11 hours of driving after 10 consecutive hours off, inside a 14-hour window. Ten and 15 belong to passenger-carrying drivers, who are on a different rule.

questions.q: A shipper delay keeps you on duty not driving for 6 hours before you ever shift into drive. How much driving can the 14-hour window still hold?
options: Eleven hours, because the delay was not driving and the 14 starts when the wheels turn
Fourteen hours, because the delay paused the window
Six hours, subtracted directly from the 11-hour driving limit
Eight hours at most
questions.explanation: Six on-duty hours leave 8 hours in the 14-hour window. You still have not used any of the 11-hour driving limit, but you cannot drive more hours than the window has left. The full 11-hour driving allowance will not fit.

questions.q: Driving has reached exactly 8 hours, with 3 hours still showing on the 11 and 5 hours left in the 14. What is the next legal driving step?
options: Take a 30-minute break before driving again
Drive the remaining 3 hours first, then take the break at the end of the day
Take a 20-minute break and continue
Stop for the day
questions.explanation: The 8-hour driving mark requires the 30-minute break before more driving. You are not out of daily time. The 11-hour maximum is still 11, and the 14 still has room, but neither lets you skip the break. Take at least 30 consecutive minutes off duty, in the sleeper, or on duty not driving before you drive again.

questions.q: After that 30-minute break, how does the next block of driving relate to the 8-hour rule?
options: The break reset the count to 14 driving hours
You may drive up to 8 more hours within your limits
The break erased the 8-hour rule for the rest of the duty period
The next block may be 11 hours without another break
questions.explanation: The 30-minute interruption lets driving time start accumulating again toward the next 8 hours. It does not remove the 11-hour cap or extend the 14-hour window. You may again drive up to 8 hours before another 30-minute break, but only inside the driving time and the window you still have.

questions.q: A 2-hour period on duty not driving is offered as the short half of a split, next to 8 hours in the sleeper. Why must it be rejected?
options: It must be rejected because sleeper time cannot exceed 7 hours
It is valid and it also zeroes the weekly on-duty total
The short period must be off duty or sleeper
It must be rejected because 8 and 2 is no longer a legal total
questions.explanation: Do not borrow the 30-minute break's on-duty option and paste it onto the split. The 2-hour piece is off duty or sleeper berth only. Eight plus those 2 on-duty hours is not a valid pair. The short period has to be off duty or in the sleeper. On-duty not driving does not qualify, even though it can count as a 30-minute break.
questions.remember: Short split period: off duty or berth.

questions.q: Six consecutive hours in the sleeper plus 4 consecutive hours off duty total 10. Why is this property-carrying split invalid?
options: The total is 10, and any two periods that add to 10 are valid
Off-duty time may not appear in a split at all
It is invalid
Neither period is at least 7 consecutive hours in the sleeper berth
questions.explanation: The long piece is not optional in type or length. You need at least 7 consecutive hours in the sleeper, not 6, plus a separate qualifying period, together at least 10.
questions.remember: Sleeper split: at least 7 in the berth.

questions.q: Ten consecutive hours off duty are broken by a 15-minute on-duty fuel stop at hour 9. Do the hours before and after the stop add to a finished reset?
options: No. The 10 hours must be consecutive, so the on-duty stop means you start the count again
Yes. Fifteen minutes is ignored inside any off-duty streak
Yes. The fuel stop counts as the 30-minute break and completes the 10
Yes. It converts the break into a 34-hour restart
questions.explanation: Consecutive is the point of the 10-hour reset. On-duty time, even a short fuel stop, breaks it. You do not add the pieces together.

questions.q: Which action hides driving and is therefore a false log?
options: Recording a real 30-minute off-duty break as off duty
Recording off duty, or sleeper, for time you were actually driving
Recording on-duty not driving while you were actually loading and not moving
Recording driving for the miles you drove
questions.explanation: False logs conceal the truth. Driving must be shown as driving. True loading is on-duty not driving. A real off-duty break may be logged as off duty. The violation is the mismatch, not the use of those statuses when they are real.

questions.q: The 11-hour driving limit is used up, the 14-hour window is not, and the driver is alert. May the property-carrying driver continue?
options: Yes, for 2 hours, under the adverse-conditions rule for being ahead of schedule
Yes, if the co-driver signs the extra miles
No. You may not drive after 11 hours of driving following the last qualifying 10-hour break
Yes, until the 14th hour
questions.explanation: Either limit can stop you. Using all 11 driving hours means you stop driving even if the 14 still has room. Being alert does not raise the 11, and another driver's signature would make a false log.

questions.q: Both the 11 and the 14 still have time, but the 60-hour limit for this non-daily carrier is exhausted. The driver feels fine. What wins?
options: The daily clocks
A 10-hour break taken tomorrow morning will have already erased today's excess
The 70-hour rule, which this carrier may use even though it does not operate every day
The weekly limit
questions.explanation: All of the limits apply. Feeling fine is not a 60-hour extension. A carrier that does not operate every day does not get to switch to 70 in 8 days to avoid the 60. You may not drive after 60 on-duty hours in 7 consecutive days when that rule applies.
questions.remember: Not every day: 60 hours in 7 days.

questions.q: An every-day operation wants to use 60 hours in 7 days for one tired driver and 70 in 8 days for everyone else. What does the rule actually assign?
options: Carriers that operate every day of the week are on 70 hours in 8 consecutive days
Each driver picks 60 or 70 each morning
Tired drivers must use the passenger-carrying 15-hour limit instead
The 60-hour rule applies only on weekends and the 70-hour rule only on weekdays
questions.explanation: The weekly rule follows the carrier's operation. Every-day operations use 70 in 8 days. Operations that do not run every day use 60 in 7. It is not a personal menu and it is not the passenger rule.

questions.q: What is the status of a 20-minute on-duty inspection after 8 hours of driving?
options: It counts as the short half of a split sleeper
It is not long enough to be the 30-minute break, and
It completes the break
It pauses the 14-hour window for 20 minutes and resets the 11
questions.explanation: Length and duty status both matter. On-duty not driving can be the break only if it lasts at least 30 consecutive minutes. Twenty minutes fails, and those minutes are still on-duty time. It is on duty it still counts against the 14 and the weekly limit.

questions.q: A qualifying adverse-conditions extension is in use. The driver also has not taken the 30-minute break after 8 hours of driving. Does the extension replace that break?
options: Yes. Weather days use a 10-minute break instead
Yes. The extension resets the 8-hour driving count to zero
No. The exception's extra time does not cancel the 30-minute break
Yes. Adverse conditions replace the break with the 2 extra hours
questions.explanation: Even when the adverse-conditions exception truly applies and adds up to 2 hours, you still need the 30 consecutive minutes before driving beyond 8 cumulative hours of driving. The exception is not a break waiver in this question.

questions.q: Which sentence correctly separates the three property-carrying rest ideas?
options: All three rests do the same job and any one of them resets every clock
The 30-minute break resets the weekly clock, and the 34-hour break only covers the 30-minute rule
Ten hours off restarts the 70, and 34 hours only resets the 11
30 minutes interrupts, 10 hours resets, 34 restarts
questions.explanation: Keep the jobs apart. The short break does not reset the 11 or the 14. The 10-hour break does not restart the weekly total. The 34-hour restart does not add hours inside a 14-hour window. Thirty consecutive minutes interrupts driving, 10 consecutive hours off resets the 11 and the 14, and 34 consecutive hours off restarts the 60/70.

questions.q: A driver logs a 34-hour restart but was driving for 5 of those hours. What is the record and the restart worth?
options: It is invalid, and the log is false
The restart is valid
The restart counts as 29 hours
The driving can be kept off the 11-hour clock
questions.explanation: A restart exists only if the 34 hours off duty really happened and were consecutive. Labeling driving as off duty to manufacture one is a false log, and it does not move the real clocks.

questions.q: You came on duty at 4 a.m. after 10 consecutive hours off. At 5 p.m. the 11-hour clock still shows 2 driving hours. How much longer may you drive?
options: Until midnight, because the date change will keep the window open
One hour, until 6 p.m
Two hours, because the 11-hour balance ignores the 14-hour window
Five hours, because a 5 p.m. stop always adds a fresh block of driving
questions.explanation: Four a.m. plus 14 hours is 6 p.m. One hour of the window remains at 5 p.m., so only one of the two leftover driving hours can be used. After 6 p.m. you may not drive, and midnight does not reset the 11 or the 14.

questions.q: At 6 p.m., 14 hours after coming on duty, 3 driving hours are still on the ELD. The driver wants a 20-minute break and then those 3 hours. Why is that plan illegal?
options: The plan is legal if the 20 minutes are logged as the adverse-conditions extension
The plan is legal for property-carrying drivers and illegal only for buses
The 14-hour window is already closed
The plan is legal
questions.explanation: This is the leftover-driving trap. Three hours on the 11 do not survive a finished 14. Twenty minutes is not the 10-hour reset and does not extend the window. The 14-hour window is already closed, and a 20-minute break neither extends it nor replaces 10 consecutive hours off.

questions.q: Which property-carrying split leaves the 14-hour window unchanged because the pair is not valid?
options: Seven consecutive sleeper hours plus 3 consecutive hours off duty
Eight consecutive sleeper hours plus 2 consecutive hours in the sleeper
Ten consecutive hours off duty
A 4-hour nap with no qualifying partner period
questions.explanation: An invalid nap stays inside the ordinary rule: it does not get excluded from the 14. Valid pairs do. A straight 10-hour break resets the 11 and the 14 instead of being calculated as a split. A 4-hour sleeper nap with no partner period that brings a qualifying total to at least 10 hours.
questions.remember: A short nap is not a valid split.

questions.q: The driver took 7 consecutive hours in the sleeper and later took 2 consecutive hours off duty, and drove several hours between them. Why does the total of 9 still fail?
options: The two periods together must be at least 10 hours, and 7 plus 2 is only 9
The periods fail
They fail because the off-duty piece had to be on-duty not driving
They succeed because each piece met a minimum and the total does not matter
questions.explanation: Meeting 7 and meeting 2 is not enough when the sum is under 10. Add enough qualifying rest in the short period, such as 3 hours off duty with the 7 in the sleeper, before you call the pair valid.
questions.remember: Sleeper split: the two add up to 10.

questions.q: After a valid split, the driver still needs a 30-minute break because 8 driving hours have accumulated since the last such break. Does the split erase that need?
options: Yes. Split drivers are exempt from the break the way a short-haul guess would be
No. The 8-hour break rule still applies
Yes. Completing a split replaces the 30-minute break for the next 14 hours
Yes. The 2-hour period always counts as every future 30-minute break
questions.explanation: The 30-minute rule is about driving time without an interruption. A split changes the 14-hour calculation when it is valid. It is not a blanket waiver of the break, and short-haul relief is not automatic.

questions.q: A short-haul story is offered: the driver stayed near the yard, so the 11-hour limit and the 30-minute break are said to vanish. What is wrong?
options: The 14-hour window vanishes too, and only the 70-hour clock remains
Near-yard trips must use the passenger-carrying 10-hour driving limit
An exception applies only when every condition is met
Nothing. Proximity to the yard is the entire exception
questions.explanation: Do not teach the short-haul details as the normal limit. Unless every condition of an exception is satisfied, the property-carrying driver keeps the 11, the 14, the 30-minute break, and the weekly cap. Being near the yard is not, by itself, the normal property-carrying rule.
questions.remember: Short-haul: every condition, or no exception.

questions.q: Required ELD on the dash, paper log in the clipboard, and the paper shows less driving than the ELD. Which record is the problem?
options: The ELD, because paper is always the controlling document
Neither, if the driver intends to reconcile them next month
The ELD, because midnight deleted the electronic miles
The paper that hides driving
questions.explanation: You do not get to pick the log with fewer hours. Concealing driving is a false log. A required ELD is not optional stationery. If an ELD is required, the paper does not replace it, and a smaller paper total is a false record.

questions.q: Which property-carrying driver is out of daily driving time but not because of the 14-hour window?
options: The driver who has already driven 11 hours
The driver who has driven 3 hours and is now at the 14th hour
The driver who has driven 8 hours and has not taken a 30-minute break
The driver who has been loading on duty for 2 hours and has not moved
questions.explanation: Eleven hours of driving ends driving even inside an open window. The driver at the 14th hour is stopped by the window instead. Eight hours requires a break but is not the 11-hour maximum. Loading is not driving time. The last 10 consecutive hours off, while the 14th hour has not yet arrived.

questions.q: Which property-carrying driver is stopped by the 14-hour window even though 3 driving hours remain?
options: The driver who completed a valid 7-and-3 split and has not yet come back on duty
The one who reached the 14th hour since the break
The driver who has driven only 3 hours and still has 11 hours of window left
The driver who finished 34 consecutive hours off this morning
questions.explanation: Leftover driving time does not survive the 14th hour. A brand-new period after 34 hours off, or after a valid split, is a different situation. Three hours of driving early in the day is not the 14th hour. The driver who came on duty after a qualifying 10-hour break and has now reached the 14th hour of that period.

questions.q: On-duty not driving for loading is logged correctly. Which clocks move, and which stays put?
options: All three pause until the trailer doors close
The 30-minute break is completed automatically by any loading, of any length
The 14-hour window and the 60/70-hour limit move
The 11-hour driving limit moves, and the 14 pauses
questions.explanation: Say it in both directions so the clocks stay distinct. Loading is on duty, so it hits the window and the week. It is not driving, so it does not hit the 11. It is a 30-minute break only if it lasts at least 30 consecutive minutes without driving. The 11-hour driving limit does not.
questions.remember: On duty: all work time, not only driving.

questions.q: A half-hour loading stop with the truck parked, status on duty not driving, comes after 8 hours of driving. Which two things are both true?
options: It satisfies the break and is excluded from the 14 the way a valid split period is
It resets the 11-hour clock
It fails the break
It counts as the break and as on-duty time
questions.explanation: On-duty not driving is one of the three ways to get the 30 consecutive minutes. That does not make the time off duty. It still consumes the 14-hour window and the 60/70 total, and it does not reset the 11. It can satisfy the 30-minute break, and those 30 minutes still count as on-duty time against the 14 and the weekly limit.

questions.q: What is left of the adverse-conditions idea after you remove late starts and heavier-than-hoped traffic?
options: Up to 2 hours, only when conditions are met
A standing 2-hour cushion every driver may use once per week
A reset of the 8-hour driving count and of the 70-hour week
Permission to log the delayed miles as off duty
questions.explanation: If you are unsure the exception applies, do not take it. It is not a weekly bonus, it does not hide miles, and it does not apply just because the day went badly. Only the case where the exception's conditions are actually met, and then only up to 2 extra driving hours and up to 2 hours on the 14-hour window.
questions.remember: Adverse conditions: up to 2 extra hours.

questions.q: Passenger-carrying drivers are different. A property-carrying driver who copies their 10-hour driving limit and 15-hour limit for a freight run is wrong because:
options: The property rule is 15 hours of driving inside 11 hours
Freight uses 11 hours of driving and a 14-hour window
Freight uses the passenger numbers whenever the trailer is empty
The property rule is 10 hours of driving inside 14 hours
questions.explanation: Match the rule to the operation. Property-carrying: 11 and 14 after 10 consecutive hours off. Passenger-carrying drivers are different: 10 hours of driving and a 15-hour limit. Do not cross them.

questions.q: Which midnight fact is safe to apply on a property-carrying log?
options: The change of date resets only the 14-hour window
The change of date completes a 34-hour restart if one hour of it was after midnight
The change of date does not reset the 11-hour driving limit or the 14-hour window
The change of date resets both
questions.explanation: Plan the day from the qualifying break, not from the log date. Midnight is not a reset and it is not a restart.

questions.q: A 10-hour off-duty period and a 34-hour off-duty period end at the same moment because the driver took 34 hours. What did the longer rest accomplish that 10 hours would not?
options: It added 24 driving hours to the 11-hour limit
It removed the need for an ELD for the next 8 days
It converted the driver to the passenger-carrying 15-hour limit
It restarted the 60/70-hour clock
questions.explanation: Thirty-four consecutive hours include a 10-hour break, so the daily clocks can start again. The part that 10 hours alone does not do is the weekly restart. Neither rest inflates an old 14-hour window. The 10 hours inside it also allow a new 11 and a new 14, without adding extra hours to an old 14-hour window.

questions.q: The driver is at 59 on-duty hours in 7 days under the 60-hour rule, then works on duty, not driving, for 3 hours. What does 49 CFR 395.3(b) allow?
options: All 3 hours of work, but no driving after 60 hours
One hour, because all work must stop at 60 hours
All 3 hours, and then 10 more hours of driving
No work at all, because 59 is treated as 60
questions.explanation: 49 CFR 395.3(b): no driver shall drive "for any period after having been on duty 60 hours in any period of 7 consecutive days". The rule bars driving after 60 hours; it does not bar other work.
questions.remember: The 60-hour limit stops driving, not work.

questions.q: Eight cumulative driving hours occurred in pieces of 3, 3, and 2, with only 10-minute stops between the pieces. Is a 30-minute break now required before more driving?
options: Yes, and the break will also reset the 14-hour window
Yes. The driving adds up across short stops
No. Each driving piece starts a new 8-hour count if you stopped at all
No. Three separate pieces can never trigger the break
questions.explanation: Cumulative means you add the driving. A 10-minute stop is not a 30-minute interruption. After 8 hours of driving, take 30 consecutive minutes before you drive again. That break will not reset the 14. Yes. The driving adds up, and short stops that are not 30 consecutive minutes do not break the accumulation.

questions.q: Which rest option is a real property-carrying split rather than the old idea that 8-and-2 is the only choice?
options: Four hours in the sleeper, which replaced both the 7-hour and the 10-hour rules
Seven hours on duty not driving paired with 3 hours of driving
Seven sleeper hours plus 3 separate hours off
Eight and 2 only, with every other total prohibited
questions.explanation: Seven plus 3 is a valid shape. Eight plus 2 can also be valid. Neither fact makes 8-and-2 the only option, and neither makes a 4-hour nap a reset. The 7-hour piece must be sleeper time, not on-duty time. Seven consecutive hours in the sleeper paired with a separate 3 consecutive hours off duty, together 10, and those periods do not count against the 14 when the pair is valid.
questions.remember: Sleeper split: at least 7 in the berth.

questions.q: You feel a 4-hour sleeper period should count as the long piece because it is 'most of 7 hours.' What does the rule require instead?
options: At least 4 hours of any duty status, which now replaces the 7
At least 8 hours off duty and exactly 2 hours on duty not driving, as the only pair
At least 34 minutes in the sleeper, one minute per hour of the restart
At least 7 consecutive hours in the sleeper
questions.explanation: Do not round 4 up to 7. A short nap is the example of a split done wrong. The long piece is at least 7 consecutive sleeper hours, the other piece is at least 2 consecutive hours off duty or sleeper, and the sum is at least 10.
questions.remember: Sleeper split: at least 7 in the berth.

questions.q: The 14-hour window has 1 hour left and the 11-hour clock has 3 hours left. The driver takes 30 minutes off duty as the required break. How much driving time remains when the break ends?
options: About 30 minutes of window
Three hours, because off duty froze the 14-hour window
Three hours plus 30 minutes
Eleven hours, because the break reset the driving limit
questions.explanation: Ordinary off-duty time does not extend the 14, including the 30-minute break. If you use part of the last hour on the break, that time is gone from the window. You cannot drive the old 3-hour balance after the window ends. The 3 hours. The break did not pause the 14, so the hour of window shrank during the break.

questions.q: Which conclusion should a property-carrying driver reach about paper logs and ELDs?
options: Hiding driving is acceptable if the hidden miles were inside the 11-hour limit
Paper does not replace a required ELD
Paper can replace the ELD whenever the paper total is lower
An ELD is optional for most drivers who must record duty status
questions.explanation: Most drivers required to keep a record must use an ELD. Do not invent exemptions. Hours that fit inside the limits still have to be recorded as the duty status you actually worked. If you are required to use an ELD, a paper log does not replace it, and editing either record to hide driving is a false log.
questions.remember: Most drivers log with an ELD.

questions.q: A Class A CDL covers a combination over 26,000 pounds when the towed unit is
options: Over 10,000 pounds
Under 10,000 pounds
Any small utility trailer
A trailer under 5,000 pounds
questions.explanation: Class A is the combination rating: GCWR over 26,000 pounds and a towed unit over 10,000 pounds.

provenance.manual: AAMVA Commercial Driver's License Manual (2025 CDL Testing System)

questions.q: A heavy straight truck over 26,000 pounds, with no trailer over 10,000 pounds, needs
options: A Class B CDL
A Class A CDL
A Class C CDL
No CDL at all
questions.explanation: Class B is the heavy straight vehicle. A small trailer does not turn it into Class A.

provenance.manual: AAMVA Commercial Driver's License Manual (2025 CDL Testing System)

questions.q: A bus built for 16 or more people can need a Class C CDL even when it is
options: Under 26,001 pounds
Over 26,001 pounds
A private passenger car
A farm tractor in a field
questions.explanation: Class C covers a smaller vehicle that carries 16 or more people, including the driver, or placarded hazardous materials.
questions.remember: Passenger vehicles: seats can require a CDL, not just weight.

provenance.manual: AAMVA Commercial Driver's License Manual (2025 CDL Testing System)

questions.q: You are driving the semi-truck labeled You. To complete this right turn safely without hitting the curb or forcing others to stop, how should you position your vehicle?
options: Swing wide to the left as you enter the intersection.
Cut the corner so your trailer wheels ride over the curb.
Move into the far left lane before starting the turn.
Turn wide as you complete the turn, rear close to the curb.
questions.explanation: CDL manual 2.7.6: if you cannot make the right turn without swinging into another lane, "turn wide as you complete the turn. Keep the rear of your vehicle close to the curb. This will stop other drivers from passing you on the right." Do not swing wide to the left as you start the turn.
questions.remember: Right turn: don't swing left first.

provenance.manual: AAMVA Commercial Driver's License Manual (2025 CDL Testing System)

questions.q: In the picture, you are the semi-truck. You and Car A arrive at this four-way stop at the same time. Who has the right-of-way?
options: You have the right-of-way because you are a larger vehicle.
Car A has the right-of-way because it is to your right.
You have the right-of-way because you are traveling straight.
The vehicle that arrived first always goes, regardless of position.
questions.explanation: At a four-way stop, when two vehicles arrive at the same time, the driver on the left must yield to the driver on the right. Car A is to your right, so it goes first.
questions.remember: A tie goes to the right.

provenance.manual: California Driver's Handbook (model handbook for general rules of the road)

questions.q: You are driving the semi-truck labeled You. Is it legal for you to pass Car A in this situation?
options: Yes, because there is no oncoming traffic visible.
Yes, if you can complete the pass within 200 feet.
No, because the double yellow line prohibits passing.
No, because semi-trucks are never allowed to pass on two-lane roads.
questions.explanation: A double solid yellow line indicates that passing is prohibited in both directions. You must stay in your lane until a dashed line or passing zone is reached.
questions.remember: Double solid: no passing either way.

provenance.manual: Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices (MUTCD)

questions.q: You are driving the semi-truck. You see ice on the road ahead in your lane. What is the safest way to handle this hazard?
options: Apply the brakes firmly before you reach the ice.
Shift to a lower gear and maintain your current speed.
Reduce speed gradually and avoid any sudden steering or braking.
Steer into the southbound lane to avoid the ice patch.
questions.explanation: When encountering slippery surfaces like ice, you should reduce speed gradually. Sudden movements can cause a heavy vehicle to lose traction and skid.

provenance.manual: AAMVA Commercial Driver's License Manual (2025 CDL Testing System)

questions.q: You are the semi-truck turning left. Car A is approaching from the opposite direction. What should you do?
options: Complete your turn quickly before Car A reaches the intersection.
Yield to Car A and wait for a safe gap before turning.
Start your turn and expect Car A to stop for you.
Honk your horn to warn Car A that you are a large vehicle.
questions.explanation: When turning left, you must yield the right-of-way to all traffic approaching from the opposite direction. Large vehicles require more time to clear the intersection.
questions.remember: Close enough to be dangerous? Let them go.

provenance.manual: California Driver's Handbook (model handbook for general rules of the road)

questions.q: You are the semi-truck. Car A is passing you on a two-lane road. What should you do to help Car A pass safely?
options: Speed up so Car A can get back behind you faster.
Move onto the right shoulder to give more room.
Maintain your speed or slow down slightly.
Flash your high beams to signal it is safe to return.
questions.explanation: When being passed, you should maintain your speed or slow down slightly to allow the passing vehicle to complete the maneuver safely and quickly.
questions.remember: Being passed? Hold lane and speed.

provenance.manual: California Driver's Handbook (model handbook for general rules of the road)

questions.q: You are the semi-truck at this T-junction. There are no stop signs or signals. Car A is approaching from your right. Who should yield?
options: You must yield to Car A.
Car A must yield to you.
The vehicle traveling faster has the right-of-way.
The vehicle on the through road always yields to the joining road.
questions.explanation: At an uncontrolled T-junction, the driver on the road that ends (the stem of the T) must yield to traffic on the through road.
questions.remember: A tie goes to the right.

provenance.manual: California Driver's Handbook (model handbook for general rules of the road)

questions.q: You are the semi-truck. You see a large pool of water in your lane. What is a specific risk for your brakes in this situation?
options: The water will cause the brake fluid to boil.
Wet brakes may pull to one side or lose stopping power.
The water will cause the tires to over-inflate.
The brakes will lock up instantly upon contact with water.
questions.explanation: Driving through deep water can cause brakes to get wet, leading to uneven braking or a complete loss of braking power. You should test them lightly after clearing the water.
questions.remember: Wet brakes? They may be weak.

provenance.manual: AAMVA Commercial Driver's License Manual (2025 CDL Testing System)

questions.q: You are the semi-truck approaching an intersection with a flashing red light. How should you proceed?
options: Slow down and proceed with caution without stopping.
Stop completely, then proceed when it is safe to do so.
Yield only if there is traffic coming from the sides.
Maintain speed as the flashing red light is for the cross-street.
questions.explanation: A flashing red light must be treated the same as a stop sign. You must come to a complete stop and yield to cross traffic before proceeding.

provenance.manual: Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices (MUTCD)

questions.q: You are the semi-truck. The intersection has a flashing yellow light. What does this mean for you?
options: You must come to a complete stop.
You should speed up to clear the intersection quickly.
Proceed with caution, scanning for hazards.
The light is broken and you should treat it as a 4-way stop.
questions.explanation: A flashing yellow light warns you to proceed with caution. You do not need to stop, but you should be prepared to react to hazards or cross traffic.
questions.remember: Flashing yellow: slow down, go with care.

provenance.manual: Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices (MUTCD)

questions.q: You are the semi-truck. Based on the pavement markings, are you allowed to pass Car A?
options: Yes, because the dashed line is on your side.
No, because the solid line is on your side.
Yes, if there is no traffic for the next half mile.
No, because passing is never allowed on a hill.
questions.explanation: When a solid yellow line is on your side of the center marking, passing is prohibited for your direction of travel.
questions.remember: Solid on your side: no passing.

provenance.manual: Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices (MUTCD)

questions.q: You are the semi-truck. Car A and Car B are already stopped at the intersection. You arrive last. What is the correct order of movement?
options: You go first because you are the largest vehicle.
Car A and Car B go together, then you go.
The cars go in the order they arrived, then you go.
Everyone must wait for a green light to appear.
questions.explanation: At a 4-way stop, vehicles should proceed in the order they arrived at the intersection. Since you arrived last, you must wait for the others to go.
questions.remember: First to stop, first to go.

provenance.manual: California Driver's Handbook (model handbook for general rules of the road)

questions.q: You are the semi-truck. The light is green, but Car A is blocking the intersection. What should you do?
options: Enter the intersection and wait there behind Car A until it moves.
Honk your horn until Car A moves out of the way.
Stay behind the stop line until there is room to clear the intersection.
Switch to the left lane and drive around Car A.
questions.explanation: You should never enter an intersection if you cannot clear it completely. Blocking the intersection ('gridlock') is illegal and unsafe.
questions.remember: No room on the far side? Do not enter.

provenance.manual: California Driver's Handbook (model handbook for general rules of the road)

questions.q: You are the semi-truck. There is an oil slick in your lane. How does this affect your following distance?
options: It has no effect on following distance.
You should decrease your following distance to stay on clear pavement.
You should increase your following distance significantly.
You should only increase distance if it is also raining.
questions.explanation: Slippery surfaces like oil slicks reduce traction and increase stopping distance. You must increase the space between you and the vehicle ahead.

provenance.manual: AAMVA Commercial Driver's License Manual (2025 CDL Testing System)

questions.q: You are the semi-truck. Pedestrian A is in the crosswalk. What is your responsibility?
options: Pedestrians must yield to large commercial vehicles.
You must stop and yield the right-of-way to the pedestrian.
You may proceed if the pedestrian is in the other lane.
Honk to let the pedestrian know you are not stopping.
questions.explanation: Drivers must always yield to pedestrians in a crosswalk, whether the crosswalk is marked or unmarked.
questions.remember: Painted or not, a crosswalk is theirs.

provenance.manual: California Driver's Handbook (model handbook for general rules of the road)

questions.q: You are the semi-truck. Car A is following you very closely (tailgating). What is the safest way to handle this?
options: Tap your brakes hard to scare the driver of Car A.
Speed up to create more distance between you.
Increase your own following distance from any vehicle in front.
Turn on your hazard lights and stop in the lane.
questions.explanation: If you are being tailgated, you should increase the space in front of your vehicle. This allows you to brake more gradually, reducing the chance of the tailgater hitting you.
questions.remember: Cut off? Drop back and make room.

provenance.manual: AAMVA Commercial Driver's License Manual (2025 CDL Testing System)

questions.q: You are the semi-truck. Car A is turning left from the opposite direction. Who has the right-of-way?
options: Car A, because left turns always go first.
You, because you are traveling straight through the intersection.
Car A, because it is a smaller, faster vehicle.
Whoever reaches the center of the intersection first.
questions.explanation: Traffic going straight has the right-of-way over traffic turning left at an intersection with no special signals.
questions.remember: Close enough to be dangerous? Let them go.

provenance.manual: California Driver's Handbook (model handbook for general rules of the road)

questions.q: You are the semi-truck. You see a yield sign at the intersection. What must you do?
options: Stop completely regardless of other traffic.
Speed up to merge before other cars arrive.
Slow down and be prepared to stop for cross traffic.
Ignore the sign if you are carrying a heavy load.
questions.explanation: A yield sign means you must slow down and yield the right-of-way to traffic on the protected road, stopping if necessary.
questions.remember: Yield sign: slow, look, stop if needed.

provenance.manual: California Driver's Handbook (model handbook for general rules of the road)

questions.q: You are the semi-truck. Car A is approaching from the opposite direction on a two-lane road at night. When should you dim your high beams?
options: When Car A is within 500 feet.
When Car A is within 100 feet.
Only if the driver of Car A flashes their lights at you.
You should never use high beams on a two-lane road.
questions.explanation: Federal rules generally require you to dim your high beams within 500 feet of an oncoming vehicle to avoid blinding the other driver.

provenance.manual: AAMVA Commercial Driver's License Manual (2025 CDL Testing System)

questions.q: You are the semi-truck. Car A and Car B are approaching from the sides. All three of you have stop signs. If you all arrive at the same time, who goes first?
options: You, because you are on the main road.
Car B, because it is to the right of Car A.
Car A, because it is to your right.
The largest vehicle always has the right-of-way.
questions.explanation: At a multi-way stop, if vehicles arrive at the same time, the vehicle to the right has the right-of-way. Car A is to your right.
questions.remember: A tie goes to the right.

provenance.manual: California Driver's Handbook (model handbook for general rules of the road)

questions.q: You are the semi-truck. The intersection has no signs or signals. Car A is to your left, and Car B is to your right. Who goes first?
options: You go first because you are in the middle.
Car A goes first because it is on the left.
Car B goes first because it is to your right.
The largest vehicle always has the right-of-way.
questions.explanation: At an uncontrolled intersection, you must yield to the vehicle on your right. Car B is to your right, so it has the right-of-way.
questions.remember: A tie goes to the right.

provenance.manual: California Driver's Handbook (model handbook for general rules of the road)

questions.q: You are driving the semi-truck across these railroad tracks. What must you not do while you are on the crossing?
options: Stay in your lane
Change gears
Keep a steady speed
Look both ways
questions.explanation: Never shift gears while crossing railroad tracks. A missed shift can leave a long vehicle stalled on the tracks. Pick a gear before the crossing that lets you clear it without shifting.

questions.q: You are hauling placarded hazardous materials and come to this railroad crossing. Where must you stop?
options: Between 15 and 50 feet from the nearest rail
Right on the first rail, then look
About 5 feet before the nearest rail
Only if a train is already in sight
questions.explanation: Vehicles that must stop at every crossing, such as placarded hazmat loads and buses, stop between 15 and 50 feet from the nearest rail, then look and listen before crossing.

questions.q: The crossing lights are flashing and a train is coming from the left. What should you do?
options: Speed up to cross before the train arrives
Cross if the train looks far enough away
Stop on the tracks to get a better view
Stop and wait until the lights stop flashing
questions.explanation: Flashing crossing lights mean a train is coming. Stop before the tracks and do not cross until the train has passed and the lights have stopped flashing.
questions.why: Expect a train on any track, at any time, from either direction.
questions.remember: Red lights flashing: wait, even if the gate goes up.

provenance.manual: California Driver's Handbook (model handbook for general rules of the road)

questions.q: Your truck has stalled on the railroad tracks. What should you do first?
options: Stay in the cab and sound the horn
Walk down the tracks to look for a train
Get everyone out and away from the tracks
Keep trying to restart the engine
questions.explanation: If you stall or get stuck on the tracks, get out and away from the tracks right away, then call the emergency number posted at the crossing.
questions.remember: Stuck on the tracks? Everyone out now.

provenance.manual: AAMVA Commercial Driver's License Manual (2025 CDL Testing System)

questions.q: Car A is driving beside the right side of your trailer. The shaded areas are your blind spots. Why is this a problem?
options: Trucks have no blind spots on the right
You may not see Car A when you move right
Car A is too far away to matter
Car A can always see your turn signals
questions.explanation: Large trucks have big blind spots, the largest along the right side. A car there can disappear from your mirrors, so check often and assume someone may be there before moving right.
questions.remember: Big blind spots: assume they're there.

provenance.manual: AAMVA Commercial Driver's License Manual (2025 CDL Testing System)

questions.q: You are entering the highway from the on-ramp. Car A is in the right lane. What should you do?
options: Adjust your speed to merge into a safe gap
Expect Car A to move over for you
Merge right away, whatever the traffic
Stop at the end of the ramp and wait
questions.explanation: Use the ramp to match the speed of traffic and merge into a gap that is large enough for your long vehicle. Do not count on other drivers to make room.
questions.remember: Merge at the speed of traffic.

provenance.manual: California Driver's Handbook (model handbook for general rules of the road)

questions.q: You are coming up on a work zone with cones along the shoulder. What should you do?
options: Drive on the shoulder to pass the cones
Use the cones as a guide to speed up
Slow down and watch for workers and lane shifts
Keep your speed so you clear it quickly
questions.explanation: Slow down in work zones, keep extra space, and watch for workers, equipment and sudden lane changes.
questions.why: Speeding is the top cause of work-zone injuries and deaths.

provenance.manual: AAMVA Commercial Driver's License Manual (2025 CDL Testing System)

questions.q: At night, a deer is standing on the road ahead. What should you do?
options: Slow down and avoid any sudden swerve
Swerve hard onto the shoulder
Flash your lights and keep your speed
Speed up to pass before it moves
questions.explanation: A sharp swerve in a heavy vehicle can cause a rollover or a crash with another vehicle. Slow down, stay in control, and expect the animal to move unpredictably.
questions.remember: Animals near the road: slow, then pass with care.

provenance.manual: California Driver's Handbook (model handbook for general rules of the road)

questions.q: You drive a 40-foot truck at 50 mph, following Car A. How much following distance do you need?
options: At least 3 seconds
At least 1 second
At least 5 seconds
At least 2 seconds
questions.explanation: Leave one second for each 10 feet of vehicle length below 40 mph, and add one second above 40 mph. A 40-foot vehicle at 50 mph needs at least 5 seconds.
questions.remember: A second per 10 feet of length, plus a second over 40.

provenance.manual: AAMVA Commercial Driver's License Manual (2025 CDL Testing System)

questions.q: School bus A has stopped ahead in the other lane with its red lights flashing and its stop arm out. What should you do?
options: Stop only if children are in the road
Stop and wait until the lights stop flashing
Pass slowly because it is in the other lane
Sound your horn and keep going
questions.explanation: On a two-lane road, traffic in both directions stops for a school bus that has its red lights flashing and stop arm out. Stay stopped until the lights stop flashing and the arm is pulled in.

provenance.manual: California Driver's Handbook (model handbook for general rules of the road)

questions.q: You want to move into the right lane. Car A is just behind you in that lane. What should you do?
options: Wait until there is a safe gap
Move over and let Car A brake
Signal and move over at once
Speed up and cut in front of Car A
questions.explanation: Check your mirrors before and during a lane change, signal early, and only move when there is enough room for your whole vehicle.
questions.remember: A signal asks for the lane; space gives it.

provenance.manual: California Driver's Handbook (model handbook for general rules of the road)

questions.q: At night, Car A is coming toward you with its high beams on. Where should you look?
options: Straight into Car A's headlights
At the center line ahead of Car A
At your own dashboard
Toward the right edge of your lane
questions.explanation: Don't look straight at oncoming headlights. Look slightly to the right, at the right lane line or the edge of the road, until the car has passed.
questions.remember: Glaring lights: eyes to the right edge.

provenance.manual: AAMVA Commercial Driver's License Manual (2025 CDL Testing System)

questions.q: Snow is falling and you are coming up on this curve. What should you do?
options: Keep your speed and steer harder
Shift to a higher gear in the curve
Slow down before you enter the curve
Brake hard once you are in the curve
questions.explanation: Slow down before a curve, especially on slippery roads. Braking hard or shifting in a curve can lock the wheels or cause a skid or jackknife.

provenance.manual: AAMVA Commercial Driver's License Manual (2025 CDL Testing System)

questions.q: You are turning right, and pedestrian A is crossing the street you are turning into. What should you do?
options: Turn wide so you pass in front of them
Wait until the pedestrian has crossed
Start the turn and pass behind them
Sound the horn so they hurry
questions.explanation: Pedestrians in a crosswalk have the right-of-way. Wait until they have finished crossing before you make the turn.

provenance.manual: California Driver's Handbook (model handbook for general rules of the road)

questions.q: An emergency vehicle (A) is stopped on the shoulder with its lights flashing. What should you do?
options: Move over a lane or slow down well below the limit
Keep your speed and stay in the lane beside it
Stop in your lane until it leaves
Pass it on the shoulder side
questions.explanation: Move Over laws require you to move out of the lane next to a stopped emergency vehicle if it is safe, or slow down if you cannot move over.
questions.remember: Flashing lights on the shoulder: move over, slow down.

provenance.manual: California Driver's Handbook (model handbook for general rules of the road)
